title: Sharing Ceph File System namespaces over the NFS protocol
content: Ceph File Systems (CephFS) namespaces can be shares over the NFS protocol using a NFS service file server. To share a CephFS namespace, you must first have a running NFS service cluster.
section_path: Sharing Ceph File System namespaces over the NFS protocol

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running, and healthy IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- An NFS cluster created using the ceph nfs cluster create command.
section_path: Sharing Ceph File System namespaces over the NFS protocol > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Important:** **Note:** Important:

- NFSv3 (version 3) is supported and enabled for clients that do not yet support NFSv4 mounts for CephFS file shares.
 
Use NFSv4 for clients and servers that support NFSv4.2 or later.
- NFS clients are unable to create CephFS snapshots through their native NFS mount. They must use server-side operator tooling for their snapshot needs.
section_path: Sharing Ceph File System namespaces over the NFS protocol > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create a CephFS share.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Due to a known issue, do not use the cmount_path option when creating an NFS share. If a value other than / is used, NFS shares that were previously defined with the / path become inaccessible.

```bash
ceph nfs export create cephfs CLUSTER_NAME BINDING FILE_SYSTEM_NAME [--readonly] [--path=PATH_WITHIN_CEPHFS]
```

In the following example, the BINDING (`/ceph`) is the pseudo root path, which must be unique, and an absolute path.
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export create cephfs nfs-cephfs /ceph cephfs01 --path=/
{
"bind": "/ceph",
"cluster": "nfs-cephfs",
"fs": "cephfs01",
"mode": "RW",
"path": "/"
}
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- The --readonly option shares a path with the read-only permission, the default being read, and write permissions.
- The PATH_WITHIN_CEPHFS can be a subvolume. You can get the absolute subvolume path by using the subvolume getpath command.
 
```bash
ceph fs subvolume getpath VOLUME_NAME SUBVOLUME_NAME [--group_name SUBVOLUME_GROUP_NAME]
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs subvolume getpath cephfs sub0
```
2. View the share block based on the pseudo root name.

```bash
ceph nfs export get CLUSTER_NAME BINDING
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export get nfs-cephfs /ceph
{
"access_type": "RW",
"clients": [],
"cluster_id": "nfsservice",
"export_id": 1,
"fsal": {
"cmount_path": "/", "fs_name": "cephfs", "name": "CEPH", "user_id": "nfs.nfsservice.cephfs"
},
"path": "/",
"protocols": [
3, 4
],
"pseudo": "/ganesha1",
"security_label": true,
"squash": "none",
"transports": [
"TCP"
]
}
```
3. List the NFS shares.

```bash
ceph nfs export ls CLUSTER_NAME [--detailed]
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export ls nfs-cephfs --detailed
{
"access_type": "RW",
"clients": [],
"cluster_id": "nfsservice",
"export_id": 1,
"fsal": {
"cmount_path": "/", "fs_name": "cephfs", "name": "CEPH", "user_id": "nfs.nfsservice.cephfs"
},
"path": "/",
"protocols": [
3, 4
],
"pseudo": "/service1",
"security_label": true,
"squash": "none",
"transports": [
"TCP"
]
}
```
4. Get the information of the NFS share.

```bash
ceph nfs export info CLUSTER_NAME [PSEUDO_PATH]
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export info nfs-cephfs /ceph
{
"access_type": "RW",
"clients": [],
"cluster_id": "nfsservice",
"export_id": 1,
"fsal": {
"cmount_path": "/", "fs_name": "cephfs", "name": "CEPH", "user_id": "nfs.nfsservice.cephfs"
},
"path": "/",
"protocols": [
3, 4
],
"pseudo": "/ganesha1",
"security_label": true,
"squash": "none",
"transports": [
"TCP"
]
}
```
5. On a client host, mount the shared Ceph File System.

```bash
mount -t nfs -o port=GANESHA_PORT HOST_NAME:BINDING LOCAL_MOUNT_POINT
```

For example,
 
```
[root@client01 ~]# mount -t nfs -o port=2049 host01:/ceph/ /mnt/nfs-cephfs
```

1. To automatically mount on boot, open and edit the `/etc/fstab` file by adding a new line.

```bash
HOST_NAME:BINDING LOCAL_MOUNT_POINT nfs4 defaults,seclabel,vers=4.2,proto=tcp,port=2049 0 0
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For NFSv3 mounts, use vers = 3.

For example,
 
```
[root@client01 ~]# host01:/ceph/ /mnt/nfs-cephfs nfs4 defaults,seclabel,vers=4.2,proto=tcp,port=2049 0 0
```
6. On a client host, mount a shared NFS Ceph File System, created with an `ingress` service.

```bash
mount -t nfs VIRTUAL_IP_ADDRESS:BINDING LOCAL_MOUNT_POINT
```

- Replace VIRTUAL_IP_ADDRESS with --ingress --virtual-ip IP address used to create the NFS cluster.
- Replace BINDING with the pseudo root path.
- Replace LOCAL_MOUNT_POINT with the mount point to mount the share on.

The following example mounts the share `nfs-cephfs` that exists on a NFS cluster created with `--ingress --virtual-ip 10.10.128.75` on the /mnt mount point .
 
```
[root@client01 ~]# mount -t nfs 10.10.128.75:/nfs-cephfs /mnt
```
section_path: Sharing Ceph File System namespaces over the NFS protocol > Procedure

title: Modifying NFS shares
content: Modify Ceph File System share parameters with a configuration file.
section_path: Modifying NFS shares

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running, and healthy IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- An NFS share created.
section_path: Modifying NFS shares > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
You can modify the following parameters in a share with a configuration file:
 
access_type
This can be `RW`, `RO`, or `NONE`. 
squash
This can be `No_Root_Squash`, `None`, or `Root_Squash`. 
security_label
This can be `true` or `false`.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: Modifying NFS shares > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. View the share block based on the pseudo-root name.

```bash
ceph nfs export get CLUSTER_NAME BINDING
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export get nfs-cephfs /ceph
{
"access_type": "RW",
"clients": [],
"cluster_id": "nfsservice",
"export_id": 1,
"fsal": {
"cmount_path": "/", "fs_name": "cephfs", "name": "CEPH", "user_id": "nfs.nfsservice.cephfs"
},
"path": "/",
"protocols": [
3, 4
],
"pseudo": "/ganesha1",
"security_label": true,
"squash": "none",
"transports": [
"TCP"
]
}
```
2. Share the configuration file.

```bash
ceph nfs export get nfs-cephfs /ceph > export.conf
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export get nfs-cephfs /ceph > export.conf
```
3. Edit the share information.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For NFSv3 mounts (NFS version 3), use protocols = 3.

```bash
{
 "export_id": EXPORT_ID,
 "path": "PATH",
 "cluster_id": "CLUSTER_NAME",
 "pseudo": "CLUSTER_PSEUDO_PATH",
 "access_type": "RW/RO",
 "squash": "SQUASH",
 "security_label": SECURITY_LABEL,
 "protocols": [
 PROTOCOL_ID
 ],
 "transports": [
 "TCP"
 ],
 "fsal": {
 "name": "NAME",
 "user_id": "USER_ID",
 "fs_name": "FILE_SYSTEM_NAME",
 "sec_label_xattr": ""
 },
 "clients": []
}
```

In the following example, the `access_type` is modified from `RO` to `RW`.
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# vi export.conf

{
"access_type": "RW",
"clients": [],
"cluster_id": "nfservice",
"export_id": 1,
"fsal": {
"cmount_path": "/", "fs_name": "cephfs", "name": "CEPH", "user_id": "nfs.nfsservice.cephfs"
},
"path": "/",
"protocols": [
3, 4
],
"pseudo": "/ganesha1",
"security_label": true,
"squash": "none",
"transports": [
"TCP"
]
}
```
4. Apply the specification.

```bash
ceph nfs export apply CLUSTER_NAME PATH_TO_EXPORT_FILE
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export apply nfs-cephfs -i export.conf
Added export /ceph
```
5. Get the updated share information.

```bash
ceph nfs export get CLUSTER_NAME BINDING
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export get nfs-cephfs /ceph
{
"access_type": "RW",
"clients": [],
"cluster_id": "nfsservice",
"export_id": 1,
"fsal": {
"cmount_path": "/", "fs_name": "cephfs", "name": "CEPH", "user_id": "nfs.nfsganesha.cephfs"
},
"path": "/",
"protocols": [
3, 4
],
"pseudo": "/ganesha1",
"security_label": true,
"squash": "none",
"transports": [
"TCP"
]
}
```

title: Windows 11 desktop client side mount options for NFSv3 fileshare
content:
Use this information to understand the client side mount options for NFSv3
fileshare.

NFSv3 (version 3) is supported and enabled for clients that do not yet support NFSv4.2 mounts for
CephFS file shares.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Mount a file share with NFSv3 Windows 11 desktop only when NFSv4.2 is not
supported on the client or server side. For more information about configuring NFS, see Configuring
NFS Service daemons.

Use the following mount client-side options to mount a file share with NFSv3 Windows 11
desktop:

```bash
Usage: mount [-o options] [-u:username] [-p:<password | *>] <\\computername\sharename> <devicename | *>
```

| Mount options | Description |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| -o rsize=size | Set the size of the read buffer in kilobytes. |
| -o wsize=size | Set the size of the write buffer in kilobytes. |
| -o timeout=time | Set the timeout value in seconds for an RPC call. |
| -o retry=number | Set the number of retries for a soft mount. |
| -o mtype=soft|hard | Set the mount type. |
| -o lang=euc-jp|euc-tw|euc-kr|shift-jis|big5|ksc5601|gb2312-80|ansi | Specify the encoding used for file and directory names. |
| -o fileaccess=mode | Specify the permission mode of the file. These are used for new files created on NFS servers. Specified using UNIX style mode bits. |
| -o nolock | Disable locking. |
| -o anon | Mount as an anonymous user. |
| -o casesensitive=yes|no | Specify case sensitivity of file lookup on server. |
| -o sec=sys|krb5|krb5i|krb5p | Specify the security mechanism for mounting an NFS share. This value can include any of the following: sec=sys: No authentication or security checks are performed. Data transfers are not encrypted. sec=krb5: Specifies Kerberos authentication for mounting the NFS share. sec=krb5i: Extends Kerberos security by adding data integrity checks between the client and server hasn't been tampered. sec=krb5p: Enhances Kerberos security by enabling data privacy, which encrypts data exchanged between the client and server. |
section_path: Windows 11 desktop client side mount options for NFSv3 fileshare

title: Rate-limiting in NFS
content:
With the rate-limiting or QoS (quality of service) feature in NFS you can control the client’s read/write bandwidth and rate-limiting of the client's input/output operations (IOPS). This function operates at share and client levels, controlling read/write requests and IOPS. QoS helps ensures that all clients accessing backend storage receives a fair share of resources.

You can enable QoS for a single node NFS server and multiple instances of NFS servers.

The QoS configuration must be stored in the RADOS object and be accessible by any NFS server within the server group. Also, each share must reside on only one NFS server within the group.

The QoS function in NFS supports both bandwidth control and IOPS control.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The rate-limiting feature is supported only for NFS version 4 and later.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS

title: Bandwidth rate-limiting
content:
NFS bandwidth rate limiting allows administrators to control the amount of bandwidth that NFS clients use when accessing or transferring data from an NFS server. This helps prevent excessive network congestion, ensures fair bandwidth distribution, and optimizes network performance for all users and applications.

The following are supported options in bandwidth rate-limiting:

Per share (export) bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per share (export). In this case, QoS makes sure that the cumulative bandwidth of all clients accessing this share does not exceed the set bandwidth. For example, if the bandwidth limit for a share is set to 100 Mbps, any client running any operation on this share is given only 100 Mbps speed.
Per client bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per client. In this case, even if the client accesses more than one share, the total bandwidth that is given to the client will not exceed the set limit. For example, if the client bandwidth is set to 100 Mbps, this client can perform operations on any share with only 100 Mbps speed.
Per share (export)-per client bandwidth control
Use this option to configure both per share maximum bandwidth and per client maximum bandwidth. In this case, the maximum client bandwidth is controlled to the set limit, while the maximum per share bandwidth is also maintained.
 
For example, if the per share bandwidth is set to 200 Mbps and the bandwidth per client is set to 100 Mbps, client A writing to this share will have a speed of 100 Mbps. If client B writes to the same share, client B will have a rate limit of 100 Mbps, as 100 Mbps is already in use by client A.

In bandwidth rate-limiting, you can configure the maximum read and write bandwidth individually. For example, you can set the maximum write bandwidth to 100 Mbps and the read bandwidth to 200 Mbps.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Bandwidth rate-limiting

title: Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting
content:
IOPS rate-limiting is a feature that controls the number of input/output operations per second that NFS clients can run on an NFS server. This helps prevent performance degradation, ensures fair resource allocation, and optimizes storage system efficiency.

Read and write operations consist of multiple underlying tasks. For example, a write operation includes four tasks: get file, open file, write file, and put file. If you set the IOPS limit to 20, only 5 IOPS allowed for each of these tasks.

The following are supported options in IOPS rate-limiting are:

Per share operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of IOPS allowed per share. In this case, QoS makes sure that the cumulative number of operations that are performed by all clients accessing this share will not exceed the given limit. For example, if the IOPS limit is set to 20, then any client accessing this share can run only 5 IOPS.
Per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of operations that are allowed per client. Regardless of the number of shares that the client is accessing, the total number of operations that are performed by the client will not exceed this limit. For example, if the IOPS limit for a client is set to 20, then this client can perform only 5 IOPS, irrespective of the number of shares it is accessing.
Per share-per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum that is allowed per share and maximum that is allowed per client operations. The total number of operations that are run by the client is controlled to the set limit. Simultaneously, QoS helps ensure the maximum operations per share limit is kept within the limits. For example, if the IOPS limit for share is set to 20 and the client limit is set to 40, then this client can run only 5 operations on the share as its limit is set to 20. The client can run the remaining 3 operations on other shares.

For IOPS rate-limiting, all operations that the client runs are counted together as a single unit.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting

title: Managing rate-limiting for NFS clusters
content:
Learn to manage the rate-limiting or quality of service (QoS) for NFS clusters.

There are 2 types of rate-limiting for NFS clusters:
- Bandwidth rate-limiting.
- Input/output (IOPS) rate-limiting.

You can enable and disable the rate-limiting feature by using the command line.
section_path: Managing rate-limiting for NFS clusters

title: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster
content: Learn to enable the bandwidth rate-limiting feature by using the command line.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster

title: About this task
content:
You can define bandwidth limits per client or share (per share) to ensure a balanced workload distribution across the cluster.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The bandwidth rate-limiting, the limit ranges from a minimum of 1 Mbps to a maximum of 4 Gbps.

**Understanding cluster-wide enforcement of bandwidth and IOPS limits**

When you enable bandwidth or input/output operations (IOPS) control on an NFS cluster, the configured limits apply cumulatively across all hosts in the cluster, rather than per individual host.

To enforce these cumulative limits, NFS services coordinate with NFS daemons running on other hosts in the cluster. This coordination ensures that bandwidth and IOPS limits are enforced consistently, even when multiple NFS servers handle client requests at the same time.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You can configure the port used for this inter-node communication by using the cluster_qos_port field in the NFS specification. The default port is 31311.

You can control how frequently NFS daemons exchange coordination messages by using the cqos_msg_interval field in the NFS specification. The default interval is 100 ms.

Alternatively, you can update the message interval by using the command-line interface.
 
```bash
ceph nfs cluster qos set <cluster_id> <msg_interval>
```

This inter-node coordination ensures accurate enforcement of bandwidth and IOPS limits across the NFS cluster.

**Cluster QoS TCP keepalive configuration**

Cluster QoS uses TCP connections between NFS nodes. To keep these TCP connections open, configure TCP keepalive parameters in the `NFS_CORE_PARAMS` section of the nfs-ganesha.conf file on all NFS nodes.

Configure the following parameters:
 
```bash
TCP_KEEPCNT = 5;
TCP_KEEPIDLE = 30;
TCP_KEEPINTVL = 2;
```
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster > About this task

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A healthy and running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- An NFS cluster.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
Run the following command to enable bandwidth rate-limiting for an NFS cluster.

```bash
ceph nfs cluster qos enable bandwidth_control CLUSTER ID qos_type:PerShare|PerClient|PerShare_PerClient [--combined-rw-bw-ctrl] [--max_export_write_bw VALUE] [--max_export_read_bw VALUE] [--max_client_write_bw VALUE] [--max_client_read_bw VALUE] [--max_export_combined_bw VALUE] [--max_client_combined_bw VALUE]
```

 Where,
 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- qos_type is the type of bandwidth control. You can select either PerShare (per share), PerClient or PerShare_PerClient based on your requirement.
 
- If the PerShare qos_type is selected, the cluster-level quality of service (QoS) configuration applies to all shares created on that NFS cluster. If combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to false, you must specify both the max_export_write_bw and max_export_read_bw parameters. Otherwise, only the max_export_combined_bw parameter is required.
- If the PerClient qos_type is selected, the cluster-level QoS configuration applies to all clients accessing shares on that cluster. If combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to false, you must specify both the max_client_write_bw and max_client_read_bw parameters. Otherwise, only the max_client_combined_bw parameter is required
- If the PerShare_PerClient qos_type is selected, the cluster-level configuration applies to all shares and all clients of that NFS cluster. If combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to false, you must specify the max_export_write_bw, max_export_read_bw, max_client_write_bw, and max_client_read_bw parameters. Otherwise, only the max_export_combined_bw and max_client_combined_bw parameters are required.
- combined-rw-bw-ctrl This parameter enables combined read and write bandwidth. If combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to true, then only max_export_combined_bw and max_client_combined_bw parameters are allowed based on QoS type.
- max_export_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth for share write per second.
- max_export_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth for share that is read per second.
- max_client_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for writing per second.
- max_client_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for reading per second.
- max_export_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for share per second.
- max_client_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for client per second.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You can specify the value as 10, 10 MB, 10 MiB, or 10 GB.

Example of bandwidth rate-limiting for PerShare, clust_nfs is the NFS cluster ID

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos enable bandwidth_control clust_nfs PerShare --max_export_write_bw 100MB --max_export_read_bw 200MB
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": false,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_iops_control": false,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_export_read_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_export_write_bw": "100.0MB",
 "qos_type": "PerShare"
}
```

Example of bandwidth rate-limiting for PerShare with combined read/write share limit

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos enable bandwidth_control clust_nfs PerShare --combined-rw-bw-ctrl --max_export_combined_bw 200MB
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": true,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_iops_control": false,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_export_combined_bw": "200.0MB",
 "qos_type": "PerShare"
}
```

Example of bandwidth rate-limiting for PerClient

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos enable bandwidth_control clust_nfs PerClient --max_client_write_bw 100MB --max_client_read_bw 200MB
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": false,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_iops_control": false,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_client_read_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_client_write_bw": "100.0MB",
 "qos_type": "PerClient"
}
```

title: Procedure
content:
Run the following command to enable bandwidth rate-limiting for an NFS cluster.

```bash
ceph nfs cluster qos enable ops_control CLUSTER_ID qos_type:PerShare|PerClient|PerShare_PerClient [max_export_iops VALUE] [max_client_iops VALUE]
```

Where,
 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- qos_type is the type of ops control. It can be PerShare, PerClient or PerShare_PerClient.
- - If PerShare qos_type is selected, then the cluster-level QoS configuration applies to all shares created on that NFS cluster. It requires the export_ops_count parameter.
- If PerClient qos_type is selected, then the cluster-level QoS configuration applies to all clients accessing shares created on that cluster. It requires the client_ops_count parameter.
- If PerShare_PerClient qos_type is selected, then the cluster-level configuration applies to all shares as well as all clients of that NFS cluster. It requires both export_ops_count and client_ops_count parameters.
- max_export_iops is the count of IOPS operations for a share.
- max_client_iops is the count of IOPS operations for a client of a share.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If this command is used to update the qos_type, make sure to update all the shares with the required parameters.

Example of IOPS rate-limiting for PerShare_PerClient, clust_nfs is the NFS cluster ID

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos enable ops_control clust_nfs PerShare_PerClient --max_export_iops 2000 --max_client_iops 3000
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": true,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_iops_control": true,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_client_combined_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_client_iops": 3000,
 "max_export_combined_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_export_iops": 2000,
 "qos_type": "PerShare_PerClient"
}
```

Example of IOPS rate-limiting for PerShare

```

[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": false,
 "enable_bw_control": false,
 "enable_iops_control": true,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_export_iops": 4000,
 "qos_type": "PerShare"
}
```

Example of IOPS rate-limiting for PerClient

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos enable ops_control clust_nfs PerClient --max_client_iops 4000
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": false,
 "enable_bw_control": false,
 "enable_iops_control": true,
```

title: Managing rate-limiting for NFS shares
content:
Learn to manage the rate-limiting or quality of service (QoS) for NFS shares.

There are 2 types of rate-limiting for NFS shares:
 
- Bandwidth rate-limiting.
- Input/output (IOPS) rate-limiting.

You can enable and disable the rate-limiting feature by using the command line.
section_path: Managing rate-limiting for NFS shares

title: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares
content: Learn how to enable bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares by using the command line.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A healthy and running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- NFS shares.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares helps control network traffic by restricting data transfer rate for NFS clients. Bandwidth rate-limiting prevents network congestion, ensures fair bandwidth distribution, and optimizes system performance.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- When you set NFS QoS bandwidth control to a very low limit, other operations on the same file may experience delays. For example, if the QoS bandwidth is limited to 10 MB/sec and you execute the du -h FILE command while the file is under active write I/O, the command may take longer to complete.
- This behavior is expected because the file is servicing throttled write operations, which can delay concurrent access.
- You cannot enable share-level bandwidth control if the cluster-level qos_type is PerClient.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
The following command enables and updates QoS bandwidth control for shares.

To enable share-level bandwidth control, you must enable cluster-level bandwidth control with qos_type PerShare or Pershare_PerClient. This command creates QOS_BLOCK in the share block.

```bash
nfs export qos enable bandwidth_control CLUSTER_ID <pseudo_path> [--combined-rw-bw-ctrl] [--max_export_write_bw VALUE] [--max_export_read_bw VALUE] [--max_client_write_bw VALUE] [--max_client_read_bw VALUE] [--max_export_combined_bw VALUE] [--max_client_combined_bw VALUE]
```

 Where,
 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- pseudo_path is the pseudo-root path. (The path must be an absolute path.)
- combined-rw-bw-ctrl enables combined read and write bandwidth control. When set to True, only the max_export_combined_bw and max_client_combined_bw parameters are allowed, depending on the qos_type.
- max_export_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth that can be used for share write per second.
- max_export_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth that can be used for share that is read per second.
- max_client_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for writing per second.
- max_client_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for reading per second.
- max_export_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for share per second.
- max_client_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for client per second.

Example for bandwidth rate-limiting for QoS type Pershare_PerClient

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs export qos enable bandwidth_control clust_nfs /export1 --max_export_write_bw 100MB --max_export_read_bw 200MB --max_client_write_bw 300MB --max_client_read_bw 100MB
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs export qos get clust_nfs /export1
{
 "cluster_enable_bw_control": true,
 "cluster_enable_iops_control": false,
 "cluster_enable_qos": true,
 "combined_rw_bw_control": false,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_client_read_bw": "100.0MB",
 "max_client_write_bw": "300.0MB",
 "max_export_read_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_export_write_bw": "100.0MB"
}
```
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares > Procedure

title: Disabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS share
content: Learn how to disable bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS shares by using the command line.
section_path: Disabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS share

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: Disabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS share > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
You can disable bandwidth rate-limiting for the NFS shares by using the following command.

```bash
nfs export qos disable bandwidth_control CLUSTER_ID PSEUDO_PATH
```

 Where,
 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- PSEUDO_PATH is the pseudo-root path. (The path must be an absolute path.)

This command disables QoS bandwidth control for shares, allowing them to use unlimited input/output bandwidth. Once share QoS is disabled, the shares will no longer follow the bandwidth values set at the cluster level.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 To use cluster level QoS bandwidth control values for share again, you can use the NFS share apply CLUSTER_ID command, with the share section not having QOS_BLOCK.

title: About this task
content:
Enabling IOPS rate-limiting for NFS shares helps control the number of input/output operations per second that clients can perform, preventing resource contention and ensuring fair usage.

To enable share-level IOPS control, you must enable cluster-level IOPS control with qos_type ,PerShare, or PerShare_PerClient.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You cannot enable export-level IOPS control if the cluster-level qos_type is PerClient.

**Understanding cluster-wide enforcement of bandwidth and IOPS limits**

When you enable bandwidth or input/output operations (IOPS) control on an NFS cluster, the configured limits apply cumulatively across all hosts in the cluster, rather than per individual host.

To enforce these cumulative limits, NFS services coordinate with NFS daemons running on other hosts in the cluster. This coordination ensures that bandwidth and IOPS limits are enforced consistently, even when multiple NFS servers handle client requests at the same time.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You can configure the port used for this inter-node communication by using the cluster_qos_port field in the NFS specification. The default port is 31311.

You can control how frequently NFS daemons exchange coordination messages by using the cqos_msg_interval field in the NFS specification. The default interval is 100 ms.

Alternatively, you can update the message interval by using the command-line interface.
 
```bash
ceph nfs cluster qos set <cluster_id> <msg_interval>
```

This inter-node coordination ensures accurate enforcement of bandwidth and IOPS limits across the NFS cluster.

content:

 Where,
 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.

- max_export_iops is the count of IOPS operations for share.
- max_client_iops is the count of IOPS operations for a client of the share.

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs export qos get clust_nfs /export1

"cluster_enable_bw_control": false,
```

```
"cluster_enable_bw_control": false,
```

title: Procedure
content:
The following command disables QoS operations control for sharing, removing any limits on the operations for shares. As a result, shares will not be subject to any cluster-level operation restrictions.

```bash
nfs export qos disable ops_control CLUSTER_ID PSEUDO_PATH
```

 Where,
 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- PSEUDO_PATH is the pseudo-root path. The path must be an absolute path.
section_path: Disabling input/output operations rate-limiting for NFS share > Procedure

title: Listing QoS configuration for NFS share
content: Learn to list the quality of service (QoS) configuration for NFS shares by using the command line.
section_path: Listing QoS configuration for NFS share

title: About this task
content:
You can list the quality of service (QoS) configuration for the NFS shares.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: Listing QoS configuration for NFS share > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Run the nfs export qos get command.

```bash
nfs export qos get CLUSTER_ID PSEUDO_PATH [--format VALUE]
```

 Where,
 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- PSEUDO_PATH is the pseudo-root path. (The path must be an absolute path.)
- VALUE is either JSON or YAML.

Example for QoS listing:
 
QoS listing with format as JSON

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs --format json
{
"combined_rw_bw_control": false,
"enable_bw_control": false,
"enable_iops_control": true,
"enable_qos": true,
"max_client_iops": 1000,
"qos_type": "PerClient"
}
```

QoS listing with format as YAML

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs --format yaml
combined_rw_bw_control: false
enable_bw_control: false
enable_iops_control: true
enable_qos: true
max_client_iops: 1000
qos_type: PerClient
```

QoS listing for a share

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs export qos get clust_nfs /export1
{
"cluster_enable_bw_control": true,
"cluster_enable_iops_control": true,
"cluster_enable_qos": true,
"combined_rw_bw_control": false,
"enable_bw_control": true,
"enable_iops_control": true,
"enable_qos": true,
"max_client_iops": 1000,
"max_client_read_bw": "100.0MB",
"max_client_write_bw": "100.0MB",
"max_export_iops": 2000,
"max_export_read_bw": "200.0MB",
"max_export_write_bw": "100.0MB"
}
```

The share will not have any bandwidth restriction in this case; that is, it will not have any cluster level bandwidth restrictions.

title: Kerberos encryption with Ceph NFS services
content:
Learn how Kerberos encryption works with Ceph NFS services.

Ceph NFS services supports secure authentication and data integrity through Kerberos, a network
authentication protocol that uses symmetric encryption and trusted third-party verification. When
Kerberos is enabled, Ceph NFS services clients and the server authenticate each other using tickets
that are issued by the Key Distribution Centre (KDC), eliminating the need for password-based
authentication over the network.

Kerberos integration with Ceph NFS services is typically configured through GSS-API (Generic
Security Services API), which allows RPCSEC_GSS (Remote Procedure Call Security by using GSS) to
handle the authentication and encryption layers. This setup supports various levels of security,
including:

- `AUTH_SYS`: Standard UNIX authentication (nonencrypted, used for
compatibility).
- `AUTH_GSS/KRB5`: Kerberos-based authentication.
- `krb5i`: Kerberos with integrity protection.
- `krb5p`: Kerberos with both integrity and privacy (encryption).

When clients mount an NFS share by using Kerberos (for example, sec=krb5, krb5i, or krb5p), all
communication is secured according to the specified level. Encryption helps ensure secure access
control and data-in-transit protection, making Ceph NFS services a viable choice for enterprise
environments requiring strong authentication and encrypted communication.
section_path: Kerberos encryption with Ceph NFS services

title: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services
content: Learn to configure Kerberos encryption with Ceph NFS services by using the command-line interface.
section_path: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running and IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Ceph NFS services are installed and configured on the server.
- A working Kerberos Key Distribution Centre (KDC).
- Ensure that the domain name is present for all the nodes in the Ceph cluster and NFS client nodes. Use the Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN).
- The NFS node is time synchronised with KDC
section_path: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Use this procedure to configure the Ceph File System (CephFS) to work with Ceph NFS services using Kerberos-based security. This setup provides strong authentication and protects client/server communication over the network.

Kerberos support in Ceph NFS services is available from version 4.0 onward. Ensure that your Ceph cluster is running a supported version of Ceph NFS services.
section_path: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Set up the Kerberos client.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The Kerberos client machine must be time-synchronised with the KDC. It is advised to sync KDC and clients by using NTP. A time difference of 5 minutes or more leads to Kerberos authentication failure and throws a clock skew error.

1. Check whether you have the following RPMs. If not, install them using the dnf install command.

```
[root@ceph-host ~]# rpm -qa | grep krb5
krb5-libs-1.20.1-9.el9_2.x86_64
krb5-pkinit-1.20.1-9.el9_2.x86_64
krb5-workstation-1.20.1-9.el9_2.x86_64
```
2. Update the krb5.conf file similar to the configuration file on the KDC server.
For example,
 
```
[root@ceph-host ~]# cat /etc/krb5.conf
# To opt out of the system crypto-policies configuration of krb5, remove the
# symlink at /etc/krb5.conf.d/crypto-policies which will not be recreated.
includedir /etc/krb5.conf.d/
[logging]
 default = [FILE:/var/log/krb5libs.log]
 kdc = [FILE:/var/log/krb5kdc.log]
 admin_server = [FILE:/var/log/kadmind.log]
[libdefaults]
 dns_lookup_realm = false
 ticket_lifetime = 24h
 renew_lifetime = 7d
 forwardable = true
 rdns = false
 pkinit_anchors = [FILE:/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt](file:///etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt)
 spake_preauth_groups = edwards25519
 dns_canonicalize_hostname = fallback
 qualify_shortname = ""
 default_realm = REALM_NAME.COM
 default_ccache_name = KEYRING:persistent:%{uid}
[realms]
 REALM_NAME.COM = {
 kdc = 10.0.10.222:88
 admin_server = 10.0.10.222:749
 }
[domain_realm]
 .REALM_NAME.COM = NAME.REALM_NAME.COM
 REALM_NAME.COM = NAME.REALM_NAME.COM
```
3. Validate the client settings.

```
[root@ceph-host ~]# kinit admin/admin
Password for admin/admin@NAME.REALM_NAME.COM:
[root@ceph-host ~]# klist
Ticket cache: KCM:0
Default principal: admin/admin@NAME.REALM_NAME.COsM

Valid starting Expires Service principal
10/25/23 08:49:12 10/26/23 08:49:08 krbtgt/NAME.REALM_NAME.COM@NAME.REALM_NAME.COM
renew until 10/25/23 08:49:12
```
2. Configure NFS specific Kerberos.

Create service principles for both the NFS server and client. The respective keys are stored in the keytab files. These principles are required to set up the initial security context (required by GSS_RPCSEC). These service principles have a format like `nfs/@REALM`. You can copy the /etc/krb5.conf from the working system to the Ceph nodes.

Perform the following 2 steps on all the Ceph nodes where Ceph NFS services containers are running and on all the NFS clients.

1. Create a service principal for the host.
section_path: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services > Procedure (part 1)

title: Procedure
content:
```
[root@ceph-host ~]# kinit admin/admin
Password for admin/admin@XYZ.ABC.COM:
[root@ceph-host ~]# kadmin
Authenticating as principal admin/admin@XYZ.ABC.COM with password.
Password for admin/admin@XYZ.ABC.COM:
kadmin: addprinc -randkey nfs/ceph-host.abc.com
No policy specified for nfs/ceph-host.abc.com@XYZ.ABC.COM; defaulting to no policy
Principal "nfs/ceph-host.abc.com@XYZ.ABC.COM" created.
```
2. Add the key to the keytab file.
In the following example, the commands are run in the NFS server by using the `kadmin` interface. The keytab operations reflect on the keytab of the NFS server.
 
```
kadmin: ktadd nfs/ceph-host.abc.com
Entry for principal nfs/ceph-host.abc.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/ceph-host.abc.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/ceph-host.abc.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/ceph-host.abc.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/ceph-host.abc.com with kvno 2, encryption type camellia256-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/ceph-host.abc.com with kvno 2, encryption type camellia128-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/ceph-host.abc.com with kvno 2, encryption type arcfour-hmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
kadmin:
```
3. Change the Ceph NFS services container settings in the Ceph environment.

1. Get the existing Ceph NFS services container configuration.

```
[ceph: root@ceph-host /]# ceph orch ls --service-type nfs --export
service_type: nfs
service_id: c_ganesha
service_name: nfs.c_ganesha
placement:
 hosts:
 - ceph-host-node1-installer
 - ceph-host-qp49z7-node2
 - ceph-host-qp49z7-node3
spec:
 port: 2049
```
2. Modify the container configuration file nfs.yaml to pass the /etc/krb5.conf and /etc/krb5.keytab files to the container from the host. NFS refers to these files at run time to validate incoming service tickets and secure the communication between NFS and the NFS client (krb5p).

```
[root@ceph-host ~]# cat nfs.yaml
service_type: nfs
service_id: c_ganesha
service_name: nfs.c_ganesha
placement:
 hosts:
 - ceph-host-node1-installer
 - ceph-host-node2
 - ceph-host-node3
spec:
 port: 2049
extra_container_args:
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro"
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro"
```
3. Make the modified nfs.yaml file available inside the `Cephadm` shell.

```
[root@ceph-host ~]# cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
Inferring fsid ff1c1498-73ec-11ee-af38-fa163e9a17fd
Inferring config /var/lib/ceph/ff1c1498-73ec-11ee-af38-fa163e9a17fd/mon.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer/config
Using ceph image with id 'fada497f9c5f' and tag 'ceph-7.0-rhel-9-containers-candidate-73711-20231018030025' created on 2023-10-18 03:03:39 +0000 UTC
registry-proxy.engineering.abc.com/rh-osbs/rhceph@sha256:e66e5dd79d021f3204a183f5dbe4537d0c0e4b466df3b2cc4d50cc79c0f34d75
```
4. Validate the file has required changes.

```
[ceph: root@ceph-host /]# cat /var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
service_type: nfs
service_id: c_ganesha
service_name: nfs.c_ganesha
placement:
 hosts:
 - ceph-host-node1-installer
 - ceph-host-node2
 - ceph-host-node3
spec:
 port: 2049
extra_container_args:
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro"
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro"
```
5. Apply the required changes to the Ceph NFS services container and redeploy the container.
section_path: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services > Procedure (part 2)

title: Procedure
content:
```
[ceph: root@ceph-host /]# ceph orch apply -i /var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
Scheduled nfs.c_ganesha update...
[ceph: root@ceph-host /]# ceph orch redeploy nfs.c_ganesha
Scheduled to redeploy nfs.c_ganesha.1.0.ceph-host-qp49z7-node1-installer.sxzuts on host 'ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer'

Scheduled to redeploy nfs.c_ganesha.0.0.ceph-host-qp49z7-node3.qizzvk on host 'ceph-host-qp49z7-node3'
```

```
[ceph: root@ceph-host /]# ceph orch ls --service-type nfs --export

service_id: c_ganesha
service_name: nfs.c_ganesha
placement:
 hosts:
 - ceph-host-qp49z7-node1-installer
 - ceph-host-qp49z7-node2
 - ceph-host-qp49z7-node3
extra_container_args:
- -v
- /etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro
- -v
- /etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro
spec:
 port: 2049
```
4. Modify the share definition to have krb5* (krb5, krb5i, krb5p) security flavor.

```
[ceph: root@ceph-host /]# ceph nfs export info c_ganesha /exp1
{
 "access_type": "RW",
 "clients": [],
 "cluster_id": "c_ganesha",
 "export_id": 1,
 "fsal": {
 "fs_name": "fs1",
 "name": "CEPH",

 },

 "krb5"
 ],
```

title: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services
content: Learn to disable Kerberos encryption on an NFS cluster using the command line.
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Running and healthy IBM Storage Ceph 9.9.09.9.1 cluster.
- Ceph NFS services is installed and configured on the server.
- Kerberos encryption enabled.
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
To disable Kerberos encryption for the Ceph NFS services, you can configure the cluster to either

- Not use Kerberos at all (falling back to `sec=sys`).
- Use Kerberos authentication (krb5) but disable privacy encryption by not using krb5p.

In both scenarios, changes to the NFS share definition are required. A system administrator must implement these changes, which involve modifying server-side configuration files typically /etc/exports.

 An alternative approach is to adjust the mount options on the client side This method is only applicable if the existing share definition on the server already includes the sys option under the sectype parameter.
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Unmount the share.

```bash
umount EXPORT_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
$ umount mnt/nfs
```
2. Modify the configuration file (ganesha.config) to remove encryption. In the `Export` section, change `SecType=sys` to disable Kerberos encryption.

```bash
SecType=”sys”
```
3. Mount the share again with the updated configuration file.

```bash
mount -t nfs GANESHA_HOST_NAME:PSEUDO_PATHMOUNT_POINT
```

For example,
 
```
$ mount -t nfs 192.168.10.10:/foo /mnt
```
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services > Procedure

title: TLS security in NFS
content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS), when used with Network File System (NFS), enables secure, encrypted communication for NFS traffic between the client and server.

TLS is a cryptographic protocol that provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for network communications. When used with NFS, TLS encrypts all traffic between the client and server. This ensures that data is not visible to intermediaries and cannot be altered in transit without detection.

TLS runs above Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) at the transport layer and establishes a secure channel between the client and server before any application data is exchanged.

A TLS handshake is the connection establishment phase. During the TLS handshake:

- The client validates the server's identity using its certificate.
- The server may optionally request a certificate from the client.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 When NFS is configured to use TLS-based transport security, the mount negotiation and all subsequent Remote Procedure Call (RPC) operations occur over this encrypted channel.
section_path: TLS security in NFS

title: TLS versus mTLS
content:
The authentication models supported by TLS are TLS and mTLS.

TLS (one-way authentication)
In TLS authentication, only the server is authenticated. The client verifies the server's certificate against a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). The server does not verify the client's identity beyond network address and application-level authentication.
mTLS (mutual authentication)
In mTLS authentication, both endpoints present certificates during the TLS handshake. The client validates the server's certificate, and the server validates the client's certificate against its trusted CA list. This ensures only authorized clients can connect.
section_path: TLS security in NFS > TLS versus mTLS

title: Use Cases
content:
This feature is essential in scenarios where secure and compliant NFS communication is required, such as:

- SAP workloads requiring secure NFS communication.
- Migration from NetApp file services to Ceph-based NFS Regional File Services.
- Environments where compliance mandates encrypted data in transit.
section_path: TLS security in NFS > Use Cases

title: Configuring share security options for NFS
content: Set share security (XprtSec) options in NFS to control how clients connect using TLS or mTLS and understand the expected behavior for different configurations.
section_path: Configuring share security options for NFS

title: About this task
content: Share security options determine whether NFS traffic uses plaintext or encrypted (TLS or mTLS) . These settings affect client mount behavior and enforce encryption policies for secure communication.
section_path: Configuring share security options for NFS > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Share security options.

```bash
ceph nfs export create cephfs mynfs /export3 myfs --xprtsec tls
```

The expected behavior based on server share security and client mount options are listed in Table 1.

| Server share security | Client mount option | Expected behavior |
| --------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| XprtSec=none | (no xprtsec) | Mount succeeds in plaintext (unencrypted TCP/UDP). |
| XprtSec=none | xprtsec=tls | Mount succeeds over TLS; encryption used even though not required. |
| XprtSec=none | xprtsec=mtls | Mount succeeds over TLS; encryption used even though not required. |
| XprtSec=tls | (no xprtsec) | Mount fails with EACCES ("Permission denied") - server rejects non-TLS connections. |
| XprtSec=tls | xprtsec=tls | Mount succeeds over TLS; server certificate validated by client. |
| XprtSec=tls | xprtsec=mtls | Mount succeeds over TLS; client certificate validation is not enforced. |
| XprtSec=mtls | (no xprtsec) | Mount fails with EACCES - client not attempting mTLS. |
| XprtSec=mtls | xprtsec=tls | Mount fails with EACCES - mTLS required; client must provide valid certificate. |
| XprtSec=mtls | xprtsec=mtls | Mount succeeds only if client presents a valid certificate trusted by the server; otherwise fails with EACCES. |

You can specify share security options manually. For more information, see Manually specify share security options for NFS.
section_path: Configuring share security options for NFS > Procedure

title: Configuring TLS settings for NFS
content: Enable and customize TLS settings in NFS to secure NFS traffic with encryption and optional mutual authentication.
section_path: Configuring TLS settings for NFS

title: About this task
content: TLS settings in NFS control how encrypted communication is established between clients and the server. When you deploy the NFS service using this specification, certificates are generated and configured automatically based on the selected certificate source. The TLS settings also define the cipher suites, minimum protocol version, and optional features such as Kernel TLS (KTLS) and debugging.
section_path: Configuring TLS settings for NFS > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Deploy or update the NFS service specification file with TLS and SSL configuration.
The following example shows an NFS service specification with TLS and SSL configuration by using inline certificates.
 
```bash
.. code-block:: yaml

 service_type: nfs
 service_id: mynfs
 placement:
 hosts:
 - ceph-node-0
 spec:
 port: 12345
 ssl: true
 certificate_source: inline|reference|cephadm-signed
 ssl_cert: |
 -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
 (PEM cert contents here)
 -----END CERTIFICATE-----
 ssl_key: |
 -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
 (PEM key contents here)
 -----END PRIVATE KEY-----
 ssl_ca_cert:
 -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
 (PEM key contents here)
 -----END PRIVATE KEY-----
 tls_ktls: true
 tls_debug: true
 tls_min_version: TLSv1.3
 tls_ciphers: AES-256
```

TLS configuration parameters and their default values are listed in Table 1.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| service_type | nfs | Defines the service type to deploy. |
| service_id | mynfs | Identifier for the NFS service instance. |
| placement | "" | Defines where the NFS service is deployed, including host selection and scheduling constraints. |
| hosts | ceph-node-0 | Host (or hosts) where the NFS service runs. |
| port | 12345 | TCP port that the NFS service listens on. |
| ssl | true | Enable or disable TLS for the NFS service. |
| certificate_source | inline | reference | cephadm-signed | Location of certificate material: inline content, external reference, or cephadm-signed. |
| ssl_cert | (PEM certificate) | Server certificate in PEM format (used when certificate_source is inline). |
| ssl_key | (PEM private key) | Server private key in PEM format matching ssl_cert. |
| ssl_ca_cert | (PEM CA certificate) | CA certificate (or chain) in PEM format used to validate the server certificate. |
| tls_ktls | true | Enable Kernel TLS acceleration if supported by the platform. |
| tls_debug | true | Enable detailed TLS debugging logs (use only for troubleshooting). |
| tls_min_version | TLSv1.3 | Minimum supported TLS protocol version. |
| tls_ciphers | AES-256 | Cipher suite policy for TLS connections. |
section_path: Configuring TLS settings for NFS > Procedure

title: Results
content: In case of configuration failure, you can configure TLS settings for NFS manually. For more information, see Manually configuring TLS settings for NFS.
section_path: Configuring TLS settings for NFS > Results

title: Setting up TLS in NFS client using Stunnel
content: Learn how to configure TLS for NFS to protect data in transit and ensure secure communication between NFS clients and servers.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS client using Stunnel

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Install TLS backend library (OpenSSL) based on your build configuration.
- The TLS certificates and keys must be available.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You must have access to the following TLS certificates:
 
- CA certificate (`ca.crt`)
- Server certificate (`ganesha.crt`)
- Private key (`ganesha.key`)
- Ensure client-side support for TLS or mTLS (NFS client tools that support `xprtsec=tls` or `xprtsec=mtls`).
 
For more information on configuring the NFS client with TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS) support How to > Enhancing security > Data encryption in transit > Establishing encryption in transit for regional file share. > Establishing encryption in transit for regional file share in Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) documentation in IBM Cloud Docs.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS client using Stunnel > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
TLS adds an encryption layer to NFS traffic, safeguarding sensitive information from interception or tampering during transmission. By enabling TLS in NFS, you can enforce secure connections, maintain data integrity, and comply with security best practices.

Use Stunnel to enable TLS in older clients without native TLS support.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS client using Stunnel > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Install Stunnel on the client side.
2. Configure Stunnel (`/etc/stunnel/stunnel.conf`) to forward traffic to the NFS port.
For example,
 
```
pid = /var/run/stunnel/stunnel.pid
cert = /home/dpp/workspace/TLS_certificates/vm1.crt
key = /home/dpp/workspace/TLS_certificates/vm1.key
CAfile = /home/dpp/workspace/TLS_certificates/ca.crt
socket = r:TCP_NODELAY=1
foreground = yes
debug = 7
output = /var/log/stunnel.log
renegotiation = no
[nfs4]
client = yes
accept = 127.0.0.1:49152
connect = 23.13.161.10:2049
sslVersion = TLSv1.3
ciphers = ALL
verify = 2
```
3. Change the `verify` value for TLS or mTLS as needed.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Optional: Remove the `cert` and `key` entries if mTLS is not required on the client.
4. Start Stunnel.

```bash
stunnel /etc/stunnel/stunnel.conf
```
5. Mount NFS through Stunnel.

```bash
mount -vv -t nfs -o rw -o port=49152 127.0.0.1:/exportfs0 /mnt/
```

You can enable TLS using tlshd (ktls-utils). For more information, see Setting up TLS in NFS clients using tlshd (ktls-utils).
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS client using Stunnel > Procedure

title: SMB cluster and share management
content:
SMB service is an open source implementation of the SMB protocol that provides file and print services between clients across various operating systems.

SMB service uses the SMB protocol to share files and printers across a network connection. Operating systems that support this protocol include Microsoft Windows, Mac OS (X), and Linux.

The Ceph MGR module for SMB provides an interface for deploying and controlling clusters of SMB services and managing SMB shares. In the `SMB manager` module, a cluster is a logical management unit that maps to one or more managed SMB services that itself is a cluster and may or may not use any high-availability mechanisms.
section_path: SMB cluster and share management

title: Enabling the SMB services
content:
Before communicating with the Ceph MGR module for SMB, it must be enabled first.
 
```bash
ceph mgr module enable smb
```

Usually, SMB shares are layered on CephFS subvolumes or subvolume groups. Do not create any SMB shares on top of CephFS root volumes. You can share a subvolume once or more within a single SMB cluster context. However, defining only one SMB share per CephFS subvolume is recommended to keep complexity low.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 NFS and SMB file services cannot share the same subvolume as mixed protocol support for NFS and SMB is not supported currently and doing so can potentially cause data corruption.

Ceph managed SMB services only support the SMB2 and SMB3 versions of the protocol. The SMB1 version of the protocol, also known as CIFS, is not supported. Systems such as the Linux kernel, provide tools for both SMB1 and SMB2+ under the CIFS moniker. Check the documentation of the software packages used to help ensure that they support SMB2+ regardless of how the tool is named.
section_path: SMB cluster and share management > Enabling the SMB services

title: Quick SMB deployment workflow
content: You can deploy SMB services using multiple methods to match your operational preferences and infrastructure requirements. Deployment options include CLI-based commands, YAML specification files, or the dashboard interface.
section_path: Quick SMB deployment workflow

title: Overview
content:
Each deployment method offers distinct advantages for different use cases:

- **CLI-based deployment** provides direct control for quick setups and troubleshooting.
- **YAML-based deployment** enables reproducible configurations for production environments.
- **Dashboard-based deployment** offers a visual interface for users who prefer graphical management tools.

 Figure 1. SMB deployment workflow

title: SMB deployment methods
content:
You can deploy SMB using one of the following approaches.

CLI-based deployment (imperative method)

Use command-line interface commands to create and manage SMB clusters and shares step-by-step. This method provides direct control and is ideal for the following scenarios:

- Quick deployment and testing scenarios
- Interactive configuration and troubleshooting tasks
- Environments where administrators prefer command-line interfaces

For detailed instructions, see Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method.

YAML-based deployment (declarative method)

Define SMB configuration in YAML specification files and apply them to the cluster. This method is recommended for the following scenarios:

- Production deployments requiring consistency and repeatability
- Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) workflows and automation
- Version-controlled configuration management
- Automated deployment pipelines and CI/CD integration

For detailed instructions, see Composing resource specifications for declarative method.

Dashboard-based deployment (UI method)

Use the Dashboard web interface to configure and manage SMB services through an intuitive graphical interface. This method is best for the following scenarios:

- Environments where users prefer graphical interfaces
- Visual monitoring and management requirements
- Quick configuration changes and updates
- Teams with varied levels of technical expertise

For detailed instructions, see Managing SMB service, shares, and clusters.
section_path: Quick SMB deployment workflow > SMB deployment methods

title: Choosing the right deployment method
content:
Consider the following factors when selecting a deployment approach:

| Method | Best For | Key Benefits |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| CLI-based (imperative) | Quick setups; testing; troubleshooting | Direct control; immediate feedback; flexible configuration |
| YAML-based (declarative) | Production environments; automation workflows | Reproducible deployments; version control; scalability |
| Dashboard-based (UI) | Visual management; mixed skill levels | User-friendly interface; visual feedback; accessibility |
section_path: Quick SMB deployment workflow > Choosing the right deployment method

title: Managing SMB clusters and shares
content:
The Ceph MGR SMB module automatically deploys logical clusters on hosts by using `cephadm` orchestration.

This orchestration is automatically triggered when a cluster is configured for at least one share. The placement field of the cluster resource is passed on to the orchestration layer and is used to determine on what nodes of the Ceph cluster SMB containers can run.

Currently, SMB services can listen on port 445 only. Due to this restriction, only one SMB server, as part of one cluster, may run on a single Ceph node at a time. Ensure that the placement specs on each cluster do not overlap.

The SMB clusters are fully isolated from each other. If there are sufficient resources in your Ceph cluster, you can run multiple independent clusters that can or cannot join the same Active Directory (AD) domains or forests. You cannot share a directory with multiple different clusters that can have different authentication modes or identity mapping schemes.

You can interact with the Ceph MGR SMB module by using the following methods.

Imperative method
This method uses the ceph smb commands to interact with the Ceph MGR SMB module.
 
For more information, see Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method.

Declarative method
This method uses the `resources specification file` either in YAML or JSON format.
 
For more information, see Composing resource specifications for declarative method.
section_path: Managing SMB clusters and shares

title: Creating SMB clusters
content:
Create SMB clusters by using the imperative method.

Create a new logical cluster, which is identified by the cluster ID value. The cluster create command must specify the authentication mode the cluster uses. Authentication mode is either custom users or groups, also known as a stand-alone server, with the `user` keyword.
 
```bash
ceph smb cluster create CLUSTER_ID {user} [--domain-realm=DOMAIN_REALM] 
[--domain-join-user-pass=DOMAIN_JOIN_USER_PASS] 
[--define-user-pass=DEFINE_USER_PASS] [--custom-dns=CUSTOM_DNS] 
[--placement=PLACEMENT] [--clustering=CLUSTERING]
```

For example,
 
```
auth_mode: user
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph smb cluster create smb1 user --define_user_pass user1%passwd --placement label:smb --clustering default

auth_mode: AD
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph smb cluster create smb1 active-directory --domain_realm samba.qe --domain_join_user_pass Administrator%RT@123 --custom_dns 10.71.34.153 --placement label:smb --clustering default
```

Table 1 lists the parameters that are required for creating the cluster.
 
| Parameters | Description |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| auth_mode | Specify either user or active-directory. |
| cluster_id | A unique string identifying the cluster. |
| clustering | Optional. Control if a cluster abstraction actually uses SMB’s clustering mechanism. The value may be one of default, always, or never. A default value indicates that clustering should be enabled if the placement count value is any value other than 1. A value of always enables clustering regardless of the placement count. A value of never disables clustering regardless of the placement count. If unspecified, default is assumed. |
| custom_dns | IP addresses to override default DNS resolvers. |
| define_user_pass | Authentication details for a user in the user-auth mode in the form <username>%<password>. This parameter accepts multiple username and password combinations. For example, --define-user-pass=alice%foo --define-user-pass=bob%bar --define-user-pass=charlie%baz |
| domain_join_user_pass | Credentials in the form <username>%<password> for joining SMB servers to the AD domain. |
| domain_realm | Required for Active Directory setups. |
| password_filter | Optional. One of none or base64. If the filter is none the password values on the command line are assumed to be plain text. If the filter is base64 the password values are assumed to be obscured with base64 encoding the string. If --password-filter-out is not specified this filter will also be applied to the output. |
| password_filter_out | Optional. One of none, base64, or hidden. If the filter is none the password fields in the output are emitted as plain text. If the filter is base64 password fields will be obscured by base64 encoding the string. If the filter is hidden the password values will be replaced by an invalid generic replacement string containing only asterisks. |
| placement | A specification for Ceph orchestration placement. |
| public_addrs | Optional. A string in the form of <ipaddress/prefixlength>[%<destination interface>]. Supported only when using SMB’s clustering. Assign virtual IP addresses that will be managed by the clustering subsystem and may automatically move between nodes running SMB containers. |
section_path: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method > Creating SMB clusters

title: Listing SMB clusters
content:
By listing SMB clusters, you can help ensure robust data protection and efficient management. The listing of cluster IDs output defaults to JSON. Select YAML encoding with the --format=yaml option.
 List all SMB clusters by using the smb cluster ls command.
 
```bash
ceph smb cluster ls [--format=FORMAT]
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph smb cluster ls
[
 "smb1"
]
```
section_path: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method > Listing SMB clusters

title: Removing SMB clusters
content:
Delete an SMB cluster by using the imperative method.
 
```bash
ceph smb cluster rm CLUSTER_ID
```

title: Procedure
content:
Create a new SMB share, hosted by the named cluster, that maps to the given CephFS volume
and path.

```bash
ceph smb share create CLUSTER_ID SHARE_ID CEPHFS_VOLUME PATH [--share-name=SHARE_NAME] [--subvolume=SUBVOLUME_NAME] [--readonly]
```

Use the CLUSTER_ID that is provided while creating the SMB cluster. For more
information, see Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method.

Table 1 lists the parameters that are required for creating the
cluster.
| Parameters | Description |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| cluster_id | A short string uniquely identifying the cluster. |
| share_id | A short string uniquely identifying the share |
| cephfs_volume | The name of the CephFS volume to be shared. |
| path | A path relative to the root of the volume and/or subvolume. |
| share_name | Optional. The public name of the share, visible to clients. If not provided the share_id will be used automatically. |
| subvolume | Optional. A subvolume name in the form [<subvolumegroup>/]<subvolume>. The option causes the path to be relative to the CephFS subvolume specified. |
| readonly | Creates a read-only share. |
