title: Removing a CephFS client from the blocklist
content:
In some situations, it can be useful to allow a previously blocklisted Ceph File System
(CephFS) client to reconnect to the storage cluster.
section_path: Removing a CephFS client from the blocklist

title: Before you begin
content:
Before removing a Ceph File System client, be sure that you have root-level access to the
Ceph Monitor node.
section_path: Removing a CephFS client from the blocklist > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Removing a CephFS client from the blocklist puts data integrity at risk, and
does not guarantee a fully healthy, and functional CephFS client as a result. The best way to get a
fully healthy CephFS client back after an eviction, is to unmount the CephFS client and do a fresh
mount. If other CephFS clients are accessing files that the blocklisted CephFS client was buffering
I/O to, it can result in data corruption.
section_path: Removing a CephFS client from the blocklist > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Review the blocklist.For
example:
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd blocklist ls

listed 1 entries
127.0.0.1:0/3710147553 2022-05-09 11:32:24.716146
```
2. Remove the CephFS client from the blocklist.

```bash
ceph osd blocklist rm CLIENT_NAME_OR_IP_ADDR
```

For
example:
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd blocklist rm 127.0.0.1:0/3710147553

un-blocklisting 127.0.0.1:0/3710147553
```
3. **Optional: **Set kernel-based CephFS clients automatically to reconnect when
removing them from the blocklist.On the kernel-based CephFS client, set the following
option to `clean` either when doing a manual mount, or automatically mounting with an
entry in the /etc/fstab
file.
```bash
recover_session=clean
```
4. **Optional: **Set FUSE-based CephFS clients automatically to reconnect when
removing them from the blocklist.On the FUSE client, set the following option to
`true` either when doing a manual mount, or automatically mounting with an entry in
the /etc/fstab
file.
```bash
client_reconnect_stale=true
```
section_path: Removing a CephFS client from the blocklist > Procedure

title: CephFS subvolume quiesce
content:
The subvolume quiesce provides enterprise-level consistency assurance for multi-client
applications with one or more subvolumes. With this feature, you can pause the input/output (IO) to
a set of subvolumes of a volume (file system). The ability to pause across all clients helps ensure
that any persistent checkpoints the application reaches before the pause are recoverable from the
snapshots that are made during the pause.

In cases where many write operations are run, CephFS snapshots do not provide strong consistent
backup and disaster recovery for distributed applications. The subvolume quiesce helps provide the
consistency that is needed at an enterprise level.

The `volumes` plug-in provides a command-line interface (CLI) to initiate and
await the pause for a set of subvolumes. This pause is called a quiesce, which is
also the command name.

The `fs quiesce` function is based on a lower-level `quiesce db`
service that is provided by the Metadata Server (MDS) daemons, which operates at a file system path
for granularity. The `volumes` plug-in maps the subvolume names to their
corresponding paths on the file system and then issues the corresponding `quiesce db`
command to the MDS.

```bash
ceph fs quiesce VOLUME_NAME --set-id ID-NAME [GROUP_NAME/]SUB_NAME... --await

# Now, you can perform actions while the IO pause is active, like taking snapshots.

ceph fs quiesce VOLUME_NAME --set-id ID-NAME --release --await
```
After the release command is successful, all members of the set are confirmed as still
paused and are released.
section_path: CephFS subvolume quiesce

title: Operations
content:
You can request the quiesce for a set of one or more subvolumes
(that is paths in a file system). This set is referred to as the quiesce set. A unique set ID
identifies every quiesce set. You can manipulate a quiesce set in the following ways:

include
Include one or more subvolumes - quiesce set members.
exclude
Exclude one or more members.
cancel
Cancel the set asynchronously aborting the pause on all its current members.
release
Release the set requesting the end of the pause from all members and expecting an acknowledgment
from all clients.
query
Query the current state of a set by ID or all active or known sets.
cancel all
Cancel all active sets in case an immediate resume of IO is required.

The operations that are listed before are non-blocking that is they attempt the intended
modification and return with an up-to-date version of the target set, whether the operation was
successful or not. The set can change states due to the modification, and the version that is
returned in the response is guaranteed to be consistent with other potentially successful operations
from the same control loop batch.

Some states are set `awaitable`. Any of the
commands that are mentioned before can be amended with an await modifier, which causes the commands
to block on the set after applying their intended modification, as long as the resulting set state
is `awaitable`. The command remains blocked until the set reaches the awaited state,
gets modified by another command, or transitions into another state. The return code unambiguously
identifies the exit condition, and the contents of the response always carry the latest known set
state.

`Awaitable` states on the diagram are marked with (a) or (A). Blocking versions
of the operations pends while the set is in an (a) state and completes with success if it reaches an
(A) state. If the set is already at an (A) state, the operation completes immediately with
success.

Most of the operations require a set-ID. The exceptions are:

- Creation of a new set without specifying a set ID.
- Query of active or all known sets.
- The cancel all.

You can create a new set by including members through the include or
reset commands. You can specify a set ID, and if it is a new ID then the set is
created with the specified members in the `QUIESCING` state.

When no set ID is
specified while including or resetting the members, then a new set with a unique set ID is created.
The set ID is known to the caller by inspecting the output through the following
command:

```
ceph fs quiesce fs1 sub1 --set-id=unique-id
{
 "epoch": 3,
 "set_version": 1,
 "sets": {
 "unique-id": {
 "version": 1,
 "age_ref": 0.0,
 "state": {
 "name": "TIMEDOUT",
 "age": 0.0
 },
 "timeout": 0.0,
 "expiration": 0.0,
 "members": {
 "file:/volumes/_nogroup/sub1/b1fcce76-3418-42dd-aa76-f9076d047dd3": {
 "excluded": false,
 "state": {
 "name": "QUIESCING",
 "age": 0.0
 }
 }
 }
 }
 }
}
```
However, in the output of this example, the set that is created successfully is already
`TIMEDOUT`. This is expected since the timeout parameter is not specified for this
quiesce, and in the output it is initialized to 0 by default, along with the expiration.
section_path: CephFS subvolume quiesce > Operations

title: CephFS subvolume quiesce parameters
content:
Learn about the different parameters that can be used while quiescing the CephFS subvolumes.

Use the following parameters that can be used while quiescing:
 
- Timeout
- Awaiting
- Quiesce-Await and Expiration
- If Version
section_path: CephFS subvolume quiesce parameters

title: Timeout
section_path: CephFS subvolume quiesce parameters > Timeout

title: Awaiting
section_path: CephFS subvolume quiesce parameters > Awaiting

title: Quiesce-Await and Expiration
content:
Quiesce await resets the internal expiration timer. This parameter allows for a watchdog approach to a multistep process under the IO pause by repeatedly --awaiting an already `quiesced` set. Consider the following example script:
 
```bash
set -e # (1)
ceph fs quiesce fs1 sub1 sub2 sub3 --timeout=30 --expiration=10 --set-id="snapshots" --await # (2)
ceph fs subvolume snapshot create a sub1 snap1-sub1 # (3)
ceph fs quiesce fs1 --set-id="snapshots" --await # (4)
ceph fs subvolume snapshot create a sub2 snap1-sub2 # (3)
ceph fs quiesce fs1 --set-id="snapshots" --await # (4)
ceph fs subvolume snapshot create a sub3 snap1-sub3 # (3)
ceph fs quiesce fs1 --set-id="snapshots" --release --await # (5)
```

**Warning:** **Note:** Warning:
 This example uses arbitrary timeouts to convey the concept. In real life, the values must be carefully chosen following the actual system requirements and specifications

The goal of the script is to take consistent snapshots of 3 subvolumes. In the example, the `bash -e ` option (1) is set to exit the script if any or the following commands return with a nonzero status.

An input/output (IO) pause is requested for the three subvolumes (2). The timeouts are set to allow the system to spend up to 30 seconds to reach the quiesced state across all members. The members stay quiesced for up to 10 seconds before the quiesce expires and the IO is resumed. The --await is also specified to only proceed after the quiesce is reached.

The script proceeds with the set of command pairs that take the snapshot and call --await on set to extend the expiration timeout for 10 more seconds (3,4). This approach gives up to 10 seconds for every snapshot but also allows taking as many snapshots as needed without losing the IO pause. This approach also helps get consistent snapshots. If you want, you can update the expiration every time you call for `await`.

If any of the snapshots get stuck and takes longer than 10 seconds to complete, then the next call to --await returns an error since the set is in the `expired` state, which is not an `awaitable` state. This helps to limit the impact on the applications in such scenarios.
section_path: CephFS subvolume quiesce parameters > Quiesce-Await and Expiration

title: If Version
content:
It is not enough to only observe the successful quiesce or release. Another client can make a concurrent change to the set.

Consider this example:
 
```bash
ceph fs quiesce fs1 sub1 sub2 sub3 --timeout=30 --expiration=60 --set-id="snapshots" --await #(1)
ceph fs subvolume snapshot create a sub1 snap1-sub1 # (2)
ceph fs subvolume snapshot create a sub2 snap1-sub2 # (3)
ceph fs subvolume snapshot create a sub3 snap1-sub3 # (4)
ceph fs quiesce fs1 --set-id="snapshots" --release --await # (5)
```

The sequence looks good, and the release (5) completes successfully. However, it can be that before snap for sub3 (4) is taken, another session excludes sub3 from the set, resuming its input/output (IO):
 
```bash
ceph fs quiesce fs1 --set-id="snapshots" --exclude sub3
```

As removing a member from a set does not affect its `quiesced` state, the release command (5) has no reason to fail. It acknowledges the two unexcluded members sub1 and sub2 and reports success.

To address this or similar problems, the quiesce command supports an optimistic concurrency mode. To activate it, pass an --if-version=<version> that compares the database version of the set and the operation only proceeds if the values match. Otherwise, the command is not run and the return status is `ESTALE`.

Every command that modifies a set returns this set on the stdout, regardless of the exit status. In the example, notice that every set carries a version property, which gets updated whenever this set is modified.

In this example, the initial quiesce command (1) would return the newly created set with ID snapshots and some version, for example, consider 13. Since no other changes are expected to the set while taking the snapshots with the commands (2,3,4), the release command (5) might look like this:
 
```bash
ceph fs quiesce fs1 --set-id="snapshots" --release --await --if-version=13 # (5)
```

This way, the release command returns ESTALE instead of 0, indicating that something is not right with the quiesce set and the snapshots are not consistent.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 When --if-version and the command returns `ESTALE`, the requested action is not run. It means that the script wants to run some unconditional command on the set to adjust the state according to the requirements.

The other use of the --if-version argument is for automation software. It is possible to create a new quiesce set with a given set ID. Drivers like the CSI for Kubernetes can use their internal request ID to eliminate the need to keep an extra mapping to the quiesce set ID. However, to guarantee uniqueness, the driver verifies that the set is new. For that, if-version=0 can be used, and it only creates the new set if no other set with this ID is present in the database:
 
```bash
ceph fs quiesce fs1 sub1 sub2 sub3 --set-id="external-id" --if-version=0
```
section_path: CephFS subvolume quiesce parameters > If Version

title: CephFS quotas
content:
Use Ceph File System (CephFS) quotas to restrict the number of bytes or the number of files that are stored in the directory structure. Ceph File System quotas are fully supported by using a FUSE client or by using Kernel clients, version 4.17 or newer. Learn how to view, set, and remove quotas on any directory in the file system.

When configuring quotas, be sure that you have the following:
 
- A running, and healthy IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Deployment of a Ceph File System.
- Root-level access to the Ceph client node.
- The `attr` package installed.

 For more information, see:
 
- Deploying the CephFS.
- The `getfattr(1)` manual page.
- The `setfattr(1)` manual page.
section_path: CephFS quotas

title: Limitations
content:
- CephFS quotas rely on the cooperation of the client mounting the file system to stop writing data when it reaches the configured limit. However, quotas alone cannot prevent an adversarial, untrusted client from filling the file system.
- Once processes that write data to the file system reach the configured limit, a short period of time elapses between when the amount of data reaches the quota limit, and when the processes stop writing data. The time period generally measures in the tenths of seconds. However, processes continue to write data during that time. The amount of additional data that the processes write depends on the amount of time elapsed before they stop.
- When using path-based access restrictions, be sure to configure the quota on the directory to which the client is restricted, or to a directory nested beneath it. If the client has restricted access to a specific path based on the MDS capability, and the quota is configured on an ancestor directory that the client cannot access, the client will not enforce the quota. For example, if the client cannot access the /home/ directory and the quota is configured on /home/, the client cannot enforce that quota on the directory /home/user/.
- Snapshot file data that has been deleted or changed does not count towards the quota.
- No support for quotas with NFS clients when using `setxattr`, and no support for file-level quotas on NFS. To use quotas on NFS shares, you can export them using subvolumes and setting the `--size` option.
section_path: CephFS quotas > Limitations

title: CephFS snapshots
content:
Use CephFS snapshots to create an immutable, point-in-time view of the file system. CephFS directory. CephFS snapshots are asynchronous, and you can choose which directory snapshots are created in.

Create snapshots in one of the following ways:

- With the Ceph Dashboard.
 
For more information, see Managing CephFS snapshots.
- By invoking the mkdir command within the .snap hidden directory
- By using CLI commands.

Snapshots can also be automatically created at specific intervals through snapshot schedules and policies.

Before creating CephFS snapshots, be sure to have CephFS deployed and root-level access to the Ceph MetaData Server (MDS) node.

The Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshotting feature is enabled by default on new Ceph File Systems, but must be manually enabled on existing Ceph File Systems. CephFS snapshots are asynchronous and are kept in a special hidden directory in the CephFS directory named .snap. You can specify snapshot creation for any directory within a Ceph File System. When specifying a directory, the snapshot also includes all the subdirectories within it.
 
**Warning:** **Note:** Warning:
 Each MDS cluster allocates the snap identifiers independently. Using snapshots for multiple Ceph File Systems that are sharing a single pool causes snapshot collisions, and results in missing file data.

 For more information, see Deploying the CephFS and CephFS snapshot schedules.
section_path: CephFS snapshots

title: CephFS snapshots usage
content:
Use CephFS snapshots for data protection and disaster recovery.
 
Data protection
Snapshots allow users to recover files from specific points in time. It is useful for creating backups without disrupting ongoing operations.
Disaster recovery
Snapshots are used for CephFS mirroring which enables to replicate CephFS data asynchronously to another Ceph cluster in another location.
section_path: CephFS snapshots > CephFS snapshots usage

title: CephFS limitations
content:
Before using CephFS, get to know the CephFS limitations.
 
Snapshot names
Snapshot names cannot start with an underscore (_) and cannot exceed 240 characters.
Performance impact
While creating snapshots is fast, the performance impact can be noticeable during heavy I/O operations due to the asynchronous nature of data flushing.
section_path: CephFS snapshots > CephFS limitations

title: Creating a snapshot for a Ceph File System
content:
You can create an immutable, point-in-time view of a Ceph File System (CephFS) by
creating a snapshot.
section_path: Creating a snapshot for a Ceph File System

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For a new Ceph File System, snapshots are enabled by default.
section_path: Creating a snapshot for a Ceph File System > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the `cephadm` shell.

```bash
[root@mds ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. For existing Ceph File Systems, enable the snapshot feature.

```bash
ceph fs set FILE_SYSTEM_NAME allow_new_snaps true
```

For
example:
```
[ceph: root@mds ~]# ceph fs set cephfs01 allow_new_snaps true
```
3. Create a snapshot subdirectory under the `.snap` directory.

```bash
mkdir NEW_DIRECTORY_PATH
```

The following example creates the `new-snaps` subdirectory, informing
the Ceph Metadata Server (MDS) to start making
snapshots.
```
[ceph: root@mds ~]# mkdir /.snap/new-snaps
```
section_path: Creating a snapshot for a Ceph File System > Procedure

title: Procedure
content:
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Attempting to delete root-level snapshots, which might contain underlying
snapshots, will fail.

Delete snapshots.

```bash
rmdir NEW_DIRECTORY_PATH
```

For
example:
```
[ceph: root@mds ~]# rmdir /.snap/new-snaps
```
section_path: Creating a snapshot for a Ceph File System > Procedure

title: CephFS snapshot schedules
content:
A Ceph File System (CephFS) can schedule snapshots of a file system directory. The scheduling of snapshots is managed by the Ceph Manager, and relies on Python Timers. The snapshot schedule data is stored as an object in the CephFS metadata pool, and at runtime, all the schedule data lives in a serialized SQLite database.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The scheduler is precisely based on the specified time to keep snapshots apart when a storage cluster is under normal load. When the Ceph Manager is under a heavy load, it’s possible that a snapshot might not get scheduled immediately, resulting in a slightly delayed snapshot. If this happens, then the next scheduled snapshot acts as if there was no delay. Scheduled snapshots that are delayed do not cause drift in the overall schedule.

Scheduling snapshots for a Ceph File System (CephFS) is managed by the `snap_schedule` Ceph Manager module. This module provides an interface to add, query, and delete snapshot schedules, and to manage the retention policies. This module also implements the ceph fs snap-schedule command, with several subcommands to manage schedules, and retention policies. All subcommands take the CephFS volume path and subvolume path arguments to specify the file system path when using multiple Ceph File Systems. Not specifying the CephFS volume path, the argument defaults to the first file system listed in the `fs_map`, and not specifying the subvolume path argument defaults to nothing.

Snapshot schedules are identified by the file system path, the repeat interval, and the start time. The repeat interval defines the time between two subsequent snapshots. The interval format is a number plus a time designator: `h`(our), `d`(ay), or `w`(eek). For example, having an interval of `4h`, means one snapshot every four hours. The start time is a string value in the ISO format, `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S`, and if not specified, the start time uses a default value of last midnight. For example, you schedule a snapshot at `14:45`, using the default start time value, with a repeat interval of `1h`, the first snapshot will be taken at 15:00.

Retention policies are identified by the file system path, and the retention policy specifications. Defining a retention policy consist of either a number plus a time designator or a concatenated pair in the format of `COUNTTIME_PERIOD`. The policy ensures that a number of snapshots are kept, and the snapshots are at least for a specified time period apart. The time period designators are: `h`(our), `d`(ay), `w`(eek), `M`(onth), `y`(ear), and `n`. The `n` time period designator is a special modifier, which means to keep the last number of snapshots regardless of timing. For example, `4d` means keeping four snapshots that are at least one day, or longer apart from each other.

For more information about snapshots, see CephFS snapshots.
section_path: CephFS snapshot schedules

title: Adding a snapshot schedule for a CephFS
content:
Add a snapshot schedule for a CephFS path that does not exist yet. You can create one or
more schedules for a single path. Schedules are considered different, if their repeat interval and
start times are different.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for a CephFS

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running, and healthy IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Deployment of a Ceph File System.
- Root-level access to a Ceph Manager and Metadata Server (MDS) nodes.
- CephFS snapshots enabled on the file system.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for a CephFS > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
A CephFS path can have only one retention policy, but a retention policy can have multiple
count-time period pairs.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Once the scheduler module is enabled, running the ceph fs
snap-schedule command displays the available subcommands and their usage
format.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for a CephFS > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the `cephadm` shell on a Ceph Manager node:For
example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Enable the `snap_schedule` module.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph mgr module enable snap_schedule
```
3. Log in to the `cephadm` shell on a Ceph Metadata Server node.For
example,
```
[root@host02 ~]# cephadm shell
```
4. Add a schedule for a Ceph File System.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 START_TIME is represented in ISO 8601 format.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule add FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH REPEAT_INTERVAL [START_TIME] --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME
```

In the following example, a snapshot schedule is created for the CephFS
`/cephfs` volume, snapshotting every hour, and starts on 27 June 2022 9:50
PM.
```bash
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule add /cephfs_kernelf739cwtus2/pmo9axbwsi 1h 2022-06-27T21:50:00 --fs cephfs01
```
5. Add a retention policy for snapshots of a CephFS volume path.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule retention add FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH [COUNT_TIME_PERIOD_PAIR] TIME_PERIOD COUNT
```

For example:
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add /cephfs h 14 (1)
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add /cephfs d 4 (2)
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add /cephfs 14h4w (3)
```

- **(1)** This example keeps 14 snapshots at least one hour apart.
- **(2)** This example keeps 4 snapshots at least one day apart.
- **(3)** This example keeps 14 hourly, and 4 weekly snapshots.
6. List the snapshot schedules to verify that the new schedule is created.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule list FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH [--format=plain|json] [--recursive=true]
```

The following example lists all schedules in the directory
tree.
```bash
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule list /cephfs --recursive=true
```
7. Check the status of a snapshot schedule.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule status FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH [--format=plain|json]
```

The following example displays the status of the snapshot schedule for the CephFS
`/cephfs` path in JSON format. If not specified, the default format is plain
text.
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule status /cephfs --format=json
```
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for a CephFS > Procedure

title: Adding a snapshot schedule for CephFS subvolume
content:
Create snapshot schedules and retention policies for directories in a subvolume,
subvolume within a default group, and for subvolumes within a non-default group.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for CephFS subvolume

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running and healthy IBM Storage Ceph cluster with Ceph File System (CephFS) deployed.
- A minimum of read access on the Ceph Monitor.
- Read and write capability on the Ceph Manager nodes.
- A CephFS subvolume and subvolume group created.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for CephFS subvolume > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Schedules are considered different, if their repeat interval and start times are different.

Add a snapshot schedule for a CephFS file path that does not exist yet. A CephFS path can have
only one retention policy, but a retention policy can have multiple count-time period pairs.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- After the scheduler module is enabled, running the ceph fs snap-schedule
command displays the available subcommands and their usage format.
- Subvolumes belonging to the default subvolume group and non-default subvolume group can be
scheduled for creating snapshots. However, the commands are different.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for CephFS subvolume > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
You can add snapshot schedules to the directories within a subvolume, subvolume in the
default group and to the subvolume in a non-default group.
- Add a snapshot schedule to a directory in a subvolume.
1. Get the absolute path of the subvolume where directory
exists:Syntax:
```bash
ceph fs subvolume getpath VOLUME_NAME SUBVOLUME_NAME --group-name SUBVOLUME_GROUP_NAME
```
Example:
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs subvolume getpath cephfs01 sub0 --group_name subgroup0

/volumes/subgroup0/sub0/db992be0-aacd-414e-8abd-e1bfeb37a4a2
```
2. Add a snapshot schedule to a directory in the subvolume:

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 START_TIME is represented in ISO 8601 format.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Path in snap-schedule command is <absolute_path_of_
subvolume>/<relative_path_of_test_dir>. Get the absolute_path of
the subvolume, from step 1.

Syntax:
```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule add SUBVOLUME_DIR_PATH SNAP_SCHEDULE [START_TIME] --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME
```
In
this example, `test_dir` is the directory for which the schedule is
added.
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule add /volumes/subgroup0/sub0/4dee0788-32a0-47e6-ac4b-bd8568a6989b/test_dir 1h --fs cephfs01

Schedule set for path /volumes/subgroup0/sub0/4dee0788-32a0-47e6-ac4b-bd8568a6989b/test_dir
```
- Add a snapshot schedule for a CephFS subvolume in the default
group:Syntax:
```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule add /.. SNAP_SCHEDULE [START_TIME] --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be left empty. There is
no dependency on `path` string value, you can define it with one of the following
characters:
/ - /..
In this example, a snapshot schedule for the CephFS
subvolume `sub0` volume is created, taking snapshots every hour, and starts on 27
June 2022 9:50
PM.
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule add / 1h 2022-06-27T21:50:00 --fs cephfs01 --subvol sub0
```
- Add a snapshot schedule for a CephFS subvolume in the non-default
group:Syntax:
```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule add /.. SNAP_SCHEDULE [START_TIME] --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME --group NON_DEFAULT_SUBVOLGROUP_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be
left empty. There is no dependency on `path` string value, you can define it with one
of the following characters:
/ - /..
In this example, a snapshot
schedule is added for the Ceph subvolume `sv_non_def_1` belonging to the non default
group
`subgroup0`.
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule add / 2M --subvol sub0 --group subgroup0
```
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for CephFS subvolume > Procedure

title: Before you begin
content: Before adding a retention policy, you must have a snapshot schedule in place.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for CephFS subvolume > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
To define how many snapshots to retain in the volume path at any time, you must add a retention
policy after you have created a snapshot schedule.

You can create retention policies for directories within a subvolume, subvolume in a default
group and to the subvolume in a non-default group.
section_path: Adding a snapshot schedule for CephFS subvolume > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
- Add a retention policy to a snapshot schedule created for a directory in a
subvolume.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule retention add SUBVOLUME_DIR_PATH [COUNT_TIME_PERIOD_PAIR] TIME_PERIOD COUNT
```

For example,
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add /volumes/subvolgroup_1/subvol_1 h 14 (1)
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add /volumes/subvolgroup_1/subvol_1 d 4 (2)
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add /volumes/subvolgroup_1/subvol_1 14h4w (3)
```

- **(1)** This example keeps 14 snapshots at least one hour apart.
- **(2)** This example keeps 4 snapshots at least one day apart.
- **(3)** This example keeps 14 hourly, and 4 weekly snapshots.
- Add a retention policy to a snapshot schedule created for a subvolume in the default
group.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule retention add / [COUNT_TIME_PERIOD_PAIR] TIME_PERIOD COUNT --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be left empty.
There is no dependency on `path` string value, you can define it with one of the
following characters:
/ - /..

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add / 5h --fs cephfs --subvol sv_sched 
Retention added to path /volumes/sv_sched/e704342a-ff07-4763-bb0b-a46d9dda6f27/..
```
- Add a retention policy to the snapshot schedule created for a subvolume group in the
non-default group.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule retention add / [COUNT_TIME_PERIOD_PAIR] TIME_PERIOD COUNT --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME --group NON_DEFAULT_SUBVOLGROUP_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be left empty.
There is no dependency on `path` string value, you can define it with one of the
following characters:
/ - /..

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention add / 5h --fs cephfs --subvol sv_sched --group subvolgroup_cg
Retention added to path /volumes/subvolgroup_cg/sv_sched/e704342a-ff07-4763-bb0b-a54j0dda7f16/..
```

title: Activating snapshot schedule for a CephFS
content:
Learn how to manually set the snapshot schedule to active for a Ceph File System
(CephFS).
section_path: Activating snapshot schedule for a CephFS

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running, and healthy IBM Storage Ceph cluster with Ceph File System (CephFS) deployed.
- A minimum of read access on the Ceph Monitor.
- Read and write capability on the Ceph Manager nodes.
section_path: Activating snapshot schedule for a CephFS > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
Activate the snapshot schedule.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule activate FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH [REPEAT_INTERVAL]
```

In the following example, all schedules for the CephFS `/cephfs` path
are
activated.
```
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule activate /cephfs
```
section_path: Activating snapshot schedule for a CephFS > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify that the snapshot schedule is activated, by using the snap-schedule
status command. For more information, see Checking status of CephFS snapshot schedules.
section_path: Activating snapshot schedule for a CephFS > What to do next

title: Activating snapshot schedule for a CephFS subvolume
content:
Learn how to manually set the snapshot schedule to active for a Ceph File System (CephFS)
sub volume.

- Read and write capability on the Ceph Manager nodes.
section_path: Activating snapshot schedule for a CephFS subvolume > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
- Activate the snapshot schedule created for a directory in a subvolume group.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule activate SUB_VOLUME_PATH REPEAT_INTERVAL
```

In the following example, all schedules for the CephFS
/volumes/_nogroup/subvol_1/85a615da-e8fa-46c1-afc3-0eb8ae64a954/.. path are
activated.
```
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule activate /volumes/_nogroup/subvol_1/85a615da-e8fa-46c1-afc3-0eb8ae64a954/..
```
- Activate the snapshot schedule created for a subvolume in the default group.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule activate /.. REPEAT_INTERVAL --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be left empty.
There is no dependency on `path` string value, you can define it with one of the
following characters:
/ - /..

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host02 /]# ceph fs snap-schedule activate / --fs cephfs --subvol sv_sched 
Schedule activated for path /volumes/subvolgroup_cg/sv_sched/e704342a-ff07-4763-bb0b-a46d9dda6f27/..
```
- Activate the snapshot schedule created for a subvolume in the non-default group:

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule activate /.. [_REPEAT_INTERVAL_] --fs CEPH_FILE_SYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME --group NON_DEFAULT_GROUP_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be left empty.

For
example,

title: Deactivating snapshot schedule for a CephFS
content:
Learn how to manually set the snapshot schedule to inactive for a Ceph File System
(CephFS). This action excludes the snapshot from scheduling until it is activated again.
section_path: Deactivating snapshot schedule for a CephFS

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A working IBM Storage Ceph cluster with a Ceph File System
(CephFS) deployed.
- Minimum of read access on the Ceph Monitor.
- Read and write capability on the Ceph Manager nodes.
- A snapshot schedule that is created and in active state.
section_path: Deactivating snapshot schedule for a CephFS > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
Deactivate a snapshot schedule for a CephFS path.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule deactivate FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH [REPEAT_INTERVAL]
```

This example deactivates the daily snapshots for the /cephfs
path, pausing any further snapshot
creation.
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule deactivate /cephfs 1d
```
section_path: Deactivating snapshot schedule for a CephFS > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify that the snapshot schedule is deactivated, by using the snap-schedule
status command. For more information, see Checking status of CephFS snapshot schedules.
section_path: Deactivating snapshot schedule for a CephFS > What to do next

title: Removing a snapshot schedule for a CephFS
content: Learn how to remove snapshot schedule of a Ceph File System (CephFS).
section_path: Removing a snapshot schedule for a CephFS

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A working IBM Storage Ceph cluster with a Ceph File System
(CephFS) deployed.
- Minimum of read access on the Ceph Monitor.
- Read and write capability on the Ceph Manager nodes.
- A snapshot schedule that is created.
section_path: Removing a snapshot schedule for a CephFS > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Remove a specific snapshot schedule.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule remove FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH [REPEAT_INTERVAL] [START_TIME]
```

This example removes the specific snapshot schedule for the
/cephfs volume that is snapshotting every four hours and that started on 16 May
2023 2:00
PM.
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule remove /cephfs 4h 2023-05-16T14:00:00
```
2. Remove all snapshot schedules for a specific CephFS volume.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule remove FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH
```

This example removes all the snapshot schedules for the /cephfs
volume.
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule remove /cephfs
```

content:
Validate the snapshot schedule, by using the snap-schedule list command. For
more information, see Listing CephFS snapshot schedules.

title: Removing a snapshot schedule for a CephFS subvolume
content:
Learn how to remove snapshot schedule of a Ceph File System (CephFS)
subvolume.
section_path: Removing a snapshot schedule for a CephFS subvolume

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A working IBM Storage Ceph cluster with a Ceph File System
(CephFS) deployed.
- Minimum of read access on the Ceph Monitor.
- Read and write capability on the Ceph Manager nodes.
- A snapshot schedule.
section_path: Removing a snapshot schedule for a CephFS subvolume > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
Remove specific snapshots schedules in any of the following ways.
- Remove a specific snapshot schedule created for a directory in the subvolume.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule remove SUBVOLUME_DIR_PATH REPEAT_INTERVAL START_TIME
```

The following example removes the specific snapshot schedule for the
/volumes/_nogroup/subvol_1/85a615da-e8fa-46c1-afc3-0eb8ae64a954/.. volume that
is taking snapshots every four hours and started on 16 May 2022 2:00
PM.
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule remove /volumes/_nogroup/subvol_1/85a615da-e8fa-46c1-afc3-0eb8ae64a954/.. 4h 2022-05-16T14:00:00
```
- Remove a specific snapshot schedule created for a subvolume in a default group.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule remove / --fs CEPH_FILESYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be left empty.
There is no dependency on `path` string value, you can define it with one of the
following characters:
/ - /..

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule remove / --fs cephfs --subvol sv_sched 
Schedule removed for path /volumes/subvolgroup_cg/sv_sched/e704342a-ff07-4763-bb0b-a46d9dda6f27/..
```
- Remove a specific snapshot schedule created for a subvolume in a non-default group.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule remove / --fs CEPH_FILESYSTEM_NAME --subvol SUBVOLUME_NAME --group NON-DEFAULT_GROUP_NAME
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The `path ( / )` must be defined and cannot be left empty.
There is no dependency on `path` string value, you can define it with one of the
following characters:
/ - /..

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule remove / --fs cephfs --subvol sv_sched --group subvolgroup_cg
Schedule removed for path /volumes/subvolgroup_cg/sv_sched/e704342a-ff07-4763-bb0b-a46d9dda6f27/..
```

more information, see Listing CephFS snapshot schedules.

title: Removing snapshot schedule retention policy for a CephFS

title: Before you begin
content:

(CephFS) deployed.
- Minimum of read access on the Ceph Monitor.
- Read and write capability on the Ceph Manager nodes.
- A snapshot schedule that is created for a CephFS volume path.
section_path: Removing snapshot schedule retention policy for a CephFS > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
Remove a retention policy on a CephFS path.

```bash
ceph fs snap-schedule retention remove FILE_SYSTEM_VOLUME_PATH [COUNT_TIME_PERIOD_PAIR] TIME_PERIOD COUNT
```

For example,
```
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention remove /cephfs h 4 (1)
[ceph: root@host02 ~]# ceph fs snap-schedule retention remove /cephfs 14d4w (2)
```

- **(1)** This example removes 4 hourly snapshots.
- **(2)** This example removes 14 daily and 4 weekly snapshots.

title: CephFS snapshot mirroring (Technology Preview)
content:
You can replicate a Ceph File System (CephFS) to a remote Ceph File System on another IBM Storage Ceph cluster. A Ceph File System supports asynchronous replication of snapshots directories.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Technology Preview features are not supported with IBM production service level agreements (SLAs), might not be functionally complete, and IBM does not recommend using them for production. These features provide early access to upcoming product features, enabling customers to test functionality and provide feedback during the development process.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 CephFS mirroring is currently available as a Technology Preview feature. In production environments, use other synchronization methods, such as `rsync`. You can combine these methods with periodic CephFS snapshots to help ensure data consistency. For more information, see Recovering a Ceph Monitor when using BlueStore.

To use CephFS snapshot mirroring, both the source and the target storage clusters must be running IBM Storage Ceph 7.0 or later.

The Ceph File System (CephFS) supports asynchronous replication of snapshots to a remote CephFS on another IBM Storage Ceph cluster. Snapshot synchronization copies snapshot data to a remote Ceph File System, and creates a new snapshot on the remote target with the same name. You can configure specific directories for snapshot synchronization.

Managing CephFS snapshot mirroring is done by the CephFS mirroring daemon (`cephfs-mirror`). This snapshot data is synchronized by doing a bulk copy to the remote CephFS. The chosen order of synchronizing snapshot pairs is based on the creation using the `snap-id`.
 
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Synchronizing hard links is not supported. Hard linked files get synchronized as regular files.

The CephFS snapshot mirroring includes features, for example snapshot incarnation or high availability. These can be managed through Ceph Manager `mirroring` module, which is the recommended control interface.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring (Technology Preview)

title: Ceph Manager Module and interfaces
content:
The Ceph Manager `mirroring` module is disabled by default. It provides interfaces for managing mirroring of directory snapshots. Ceph Manager interfaces are mostly wrappers around monitor commands for managing CephFS mirroring. They are the recommended control interface.

The Ceph Manager `mirroring` module is implemented as a Ceph Manager plugin. It is responsible for assigning directories to the `cephfs-mirror` daemons for synchronization.

The Ceph Manager `mirroring` module also provides a family of commands to control mirroring of directory snapshots. The `mirroring` module does not manage the `cephfs-mirror` daemons. The stopping, starting, restarting, and enabling of the `cephfs-mirror` daemons is controlled by `systemctl`, but managed by `cephadm`.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Mirroring module commands use the `fs snapshot mirror` prefix as compared to the monitor commands with the `fs mirror` prefix. Assure that you are using the module command prefix to control the mirroring of directory snapshots.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring (Technology Preview) > Ceph Manager Module and interfaces

title: Snapshot incarnation
content:
A snapshot might be deleted and created again with the same name and different content. The user could synchronize an "old" snapshot earlier and create the snapshot again when the mirroring was disabled. Using snapshot names to infer the point-of-continuation results in the “new” snapshot, an incarnation, never getting picked up for synchronization.

Snapshots on the secondary file system store the `snap-id` of the snapshot it was synchronized from. This metadata is stored in the `SnapInfo` structure on the Ceph Metadata Server.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring (Technology Preview) > Snapshot incarnation

title: High availability
content:
You can deploy multiple `cephfs-mirror` daemons on two or more nodes to achieve concurrency in synchronization of directory snapshots. When `cephfs-mirror` daemons are deployed or terminated, the Ceph Manager `mirroring` module discovers the modified set of `cephfs-mirror` daemons and rebalances the directory assignment amongst the new set thus providing high availability.

`cephfs-mirror` daemons share the synchronization load by using a simple M/N policy, where M is the number of directories and N is the number of `cephfs-mirror` daemons.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring (Technology Preview) > High availability

title: Readdition of Ceph File System mirror peers
content:
When readding or reassigning a peer to a CephFS in another cluster, make sure that all mirror daemons stopped synchronization to the peer. You can verify readdition of CephFS mirror peers with the fs mirror status command. The Peer UUID does not show up in the command output.

Purge synchronized directories from the peer before readding it to another CephFS, especially those directories that might exist in the new primary file system. Purging synchronized directories is not required if you are readding a peer to the same primary file system it was earlier synchronized from.

For more information about the fs mirror status command, see Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring (Technology Preview) > Readdition of Ceph File System mirror peers

title: Configuring a snapshot mirror for a Ceph File System
content: Learn how to configure a Ceph File System (CephFS) for mirroring to replicate snapshots to another CephFS on a remote IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
section_path: Configuring a snapshot mirror for a Ceph File System

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- The source and the target storage clusters must be healthy and running the latest IBM Storage Ceph version.
- Root-level access to a Ceph Monitor node in the source and the target storage clusters.
- At least one CephFS deployed on your storage cluster.
section_path: Configuring a snapshot mirror for a Ceph File System > Before you begin

title: About this task
content: The time taken for synchronizing to a remote storage cluster depends on the file size and the total number of files in the mirroring path.
section_path: Configuring a snapshot mirror for a Ceph File System > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the `cephadm` shell.
For example,
 
```bash
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. On the source storage cluster, deploy the CephFS mirroring daemon.
This command creates a Ceph user called `cephfs-mirror` and deploys the `cephfs-mirror` daemon on the given node.
 
```bash
ceph orch apply cephfs-mirror ["NODE_NAME"]
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply cephfs-mirror "node1.example.com"
Scheduled cephfs-mirror update...
```

1. **Optional: **
Deploy multiple CephFS mirroring daemons and achieve high availability.

```bash
ceph orch apply cephfs-mirror --placement="PLACEMENT_SPECIFICATION"
```

The following example deploys three `cephfs-mirror` daemons on different hosts.
 
**Warning:** **Note:** Warning:
 Do not separate the hosts with commas. Using commas results in the following error:
 
```
Error EINVAL: name component must include only a-z, 0-9, and -
```

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply cephfs-mirror --placement="3 host1 host2 host3"
Scheduled cephfs-mirror update...
```
3. On the target storage cluster, create a user for each CephFS peer.

```bash
ceph fs authorize FILE_SYSTEM_NAME CLIENT_NAME / rwps
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs authorize cephfs client.mirror_remote / rwps
[client.mirror_remote]
 key = AQCjZ5Jg739AAxAAxduIKoTZbiFJ0lgose8luQ==
```
4. On the source storage cluster, enable the CephFS mirroring module.

```bash
ceph mgr module enable mirroring
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph mgr module enable mirroring
```
5. On the source storage cluster, enable mirroring on a Ceph File System.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror enable FILE_SYSTEM_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror enable cephfs
```

1. **Optional: **
Disable snapshot mirroring.

**Warning:** **Note:** Warning:
 Disabling snapshot mirroring on a file system removes the configured peers. You have to import the peers again by bootstrapping them.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror disable FILE_SYSTEM_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror disable cephfs
```
6. Prepare the target peer storage cluster.

1. On a target node, enable the `mirroring` Ceph Manager module.

```bash
ceph mgr module enable mirroring
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph mgr module enable mirroring
```
2. On the same target node, create the peer bootstrap.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_bootstrap create FILE_SYSTEM_NAME CLIENT_NAME SITE_NAME
```

The SITE_NAME is a user-defined string to identify the target storage cluster.

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_bootstrap create cephfs client.mirror_remote remote-site
{"token": ""}
```
3. Copy the token string between the double quotes, from step 6.b for use in step 7.
7. On the source storage cluster, import the bootstrap token from the target storage cluster.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_bootstrap import FILE_SYSTEM_NAME TOKEN
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_bootstrap import cephfs 
```
8. On the source storage cluster, list the CephFS mirror peers.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_list FILE_SYSTEM_NAME
```
section_path: Configuring a snapshot mirror for a Ceph File System > Procedure (part 1)

title: Procedure
content:
For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_list cephfs
{"e5ecb883-097d-492d-b026-a585d1d7da79": {"client_name": "client.mirror_remote", "site_name": "remote-site", "fs_name": "cephfs", "mon_host": "[v2:10.0.211.54:3300/0,v1:10.0.211.54:6789/0] [v2:10.0.210.56:3300/0,v1:10.0.210.56:6789/0] [v2:10.0.210.65:3300/0,v1:10.0.210.65:6789/0]"}}
```

1. **Optional: **
Remove a snapshot peer.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_remove FILE_SYSTEM_NAME PEER_UUID
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For more information about how to find the peer UUID value, see step 4 of Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System.

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror peer_remove cephfs e5ecb883-097d-492d-b026-a585d1d7da79
```
9. On the source storage cluster, configure a directory for snapshot mirroring.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror add FILE_SYSTEM_NAME PATH
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Only absolute paths inside the Ceph File System are valid.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The Ceph Manager `mirroring` module normalizes the path. For example, the `/d1/d2/../dN` directories are equivalent to `/d1/d2`. Once a directory has been added for mirroring, its ancestor directories and subdirectories are prevented from being added for mirroring.

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror add cephfs /volumes/_nogroup/subvol_1
```

1. **Optional: **
Stop snapshot mirroring for a directory.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror remove FILE_SYSTEM_NAME PATH
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror remove cephfs /home/user1
```
section_path: Configuring a snapshot mirror for a Ceph File System > Procedure (part 2)

title: Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System
content: The Ceph File System (CephFS) mirror daemon (`cephfs-mirror`) gets asynchronous notifications about changes in the CephFS mirroring status, along with peer updates. The CephFS mirroring module provides a mirror daemon status interface to check mirror daemon status.
section_path: Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- A minimum of one deployment of a Ceph File System with mirroring enabled.
- Root-level access to the node running the CephFS mirroring daemon.
section_path: Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System > Before you begin

title: About this task
content: For more detailed information, you can query the `cephfs-mirror` admin socket with commands to retrieve the mirror status and peer status.
section_path: Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the `cephadm` shell.
For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Check the `cephfs-mirror` daemon status.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For more detailed information, use the admin socket interface as detailed in step 5.

```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror daemon status
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror daemon status
[
 {
 "daemon_id": 15594,
 "filesystems": [
 {
 "filesystem_id": 1,
 "name": "cephfs",
 "directory_count": 1,
 "peers": [
 {
 "uuid": "e5ecb883-097d-492d-b026-a585d1d7da79",
 "remote": {
 "client_name": "client.mirror_remote",
 "cluster_name": "remote-site",
 "fs_name": "cephfs"
 },
 "stats": {
 "failure_count": 1,
 "recovery_count": 0
 }
 }
 ]
 }
 ]
 }
]
```
3. Find the Ceph File System ID on the node running the CephFS mirroring daemon.

```bash
ceph --admin-daemon PATH_TO_THE_ASOK_FILE help
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 When mirroring is disabled, the respective fs mirror status command for the file system does not show up in the help command.

In the following example, the Ceph File System ID is `cephfs@11`.
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph --admin-daemon /var/run/ceph/1011435c-9e30-4db6-b720-5bf482006e0e/ceph-client.cephfs-mirror.node1.bndvox.asok help
{
 ...
 "fs mirror peer status cephfs@11 1011435c-9e30-4db6-b720-5bf482006e0e": "get peer mirror status",
 "fs mirror status cephfs@11": "get filesystem mirror status",
 ...
}
```
4. View the mirror status.

```bash
ceph --admin-daemon PATH_TO_THE_ASOK_FILE fs mirror status FILE_SYSTEM_NAME @_FILE_SYSTEM_ID
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph --admin-daemon /var/run/ceph/1011435c-9e30-4db6-b720-5bf482006e0e/ceph-client.cephfs-mirror.node1.bndvox.asok fs mirror status cephfs@11
{
 "rados_inst": "192.168.0.5:0/1476644347",
 "peers": {
 "1011435c-9e30-4db6-b720-5bf482006e0e": { (1)
 "remote": {
 "client_name": "client.mirror_remote",
 "cluster_name": "remote-site",
 "fs_name": "cephfs"
 }
 }
 },
 "snap_dirs": {
 "dir_count": 1
 }
}
```

- **(1)** This is the unique peer UUID.
5. View the peer status.

```bash
ceph --admin-daemon PATH_TO_ADMIN_SOCKET fs mirror status FILE_SYSTEM_NAME@FILE_SYSTEM_ID PEER_UUID
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph --admin-daemon /var/run/ceph/cephfs-mirror.asok fs mirror peer status cephfs@11 1011435c-9e30-4db6-b720-5bf482006e0e
{
 "/home/user1": {
 "state": "idle", (1)
 "last_synced_snap": {
 "id": 120,
 "name": "snap1",
 "sync_duration": 0.079997898999999997,
 "sync_time_stamp": "274900.558797s"
 },
 "snaps_synced": 2, (2)
 "snaps_deleted": 0, (3)
 "snaps_renamed": 0
 }
}
```

The `state` can be one of these three values:
 
- **(1)** `idle` means that the directory is currently not being synchronized.
- **(2)** `syncing` means that the directory is currently being synchronized.
- **(3)** `failed` means that the directory has reached the upper limit of consecutive failures.

 The default number of consecutive failures is 10, and the default retry interval is 60 seconds.
section_path: Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System > Procedure

title: Displaying the directory to which cephfs-mirror daemon is mapped
content:
To display the directory to which `cephfs-mirror` daemon is mapped:
 
```bash
ceph fs snapshot mirror dirmap FILE_SYSTEM_NAME PATH
```

Example 1 (mirror daemons are running)

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror dirmap cephfs /volumes/_nogroup/subvol_1
{
 "instance_id": "25184", (1)
 "last_shuffled": 1661162007.012663,
 "state": "mapped"
}
```

- **(1)** `instance_id` is the RADOS instance-ID that is associated with a `cephfs-mirror` daemon.

Example 2 (no mirror daemons are running)

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs snapshot mirror dirmap cephfs /volumes/_nogroup/subvol_1
{
 "reason": "no mirror daemons running",
 "state": "stalled" (1)
}
```

- **(1)** `stalled` state means the CephFS mirroring is stalled.
section_path: Viewing the mirror status for a Ceph File System > Displaying the directory to which cephfs-mirror daemon is mapped

title: Viewing metrics for Ceph File System snapshot mirroring
content: Viewing these metrics helps in monitoring the performance and the sync progress.
section_path: Viewing metrics for Ceph File System snapshot mirroring

title: Before you begin
content:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- A minimum of one deployment of a Ceph File System snapshot mirroring enabled.
- Root-level access to the node running the Ceph File System mirroring daemon.
section_path: Viewing metrics for Ceph File System snapshot mirroring > Before you begin

title: About this task
content: Check Ceph File System snapshot mirror health and volume metrics by using the counter dump.
section_path: Viewing metrics for Ceph File System snapshot mirroring > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Get the name of the `asok` file. The `asok` file is available where the mirroring daemon is running and is located at /var/run/ceph/ within the `cephadm` shell.
2. Check the mirroring metrics and synchronization status by running the following command on the node running the CephFS mirroring daemon.
Syntax:
 
```bash
[ceph: root@mirror-host01 /]# ceph --admin-daemon ASOK_FILE_NAME counter dump
```

Example:
 
```
[ceph: root@mirror-host01 /]# ceph --admin-daemon ceph-client.cephfs-mirror.ceph1-hk-n-0mfqao-node7.pnbrlu.2.93909288073464.asok counter dump

[
 {
 "key": "cephfs_mirror",
 "value": [
 {
 "labels": {},
 "counters": {
 "mirrored_filesystems": 1,
 "mirror_enable_failures": 0
 }
 }
 ]
```

title: Snapshot visibility for CephFS and NFS clients
content: CephFS controls snapshot (.snap) directory visibility for subvolumes and NFS shares, and how clients enforce visibility rules.
section_path: Snapshot visibility for CephFS and NFS clients

title: Snapshot visibility overview
content:
CephFS supports snapshots at the subvolume level. Snapshots are stored inside the special directory named .snap, which is visible to clients by default. Administrators can control whether this directory is visible to clients by configuring:
 
- Subvolume‑level snapshot visibility flag
- Client‑side adherence to visibility rules
- Share‑level snapshot visibility toggle for NFS

 These controls allow administrators to hide or expose snapshots to specific NFS clients or subvolumes.
section_path: Snapshot visibility for CephFS and NFS clients > Snapshot visibility overview

title: How snapshot visibility works at subvolume, client, and share levels
content:
Snapshot visibility in CephFS is determined by the interaction of three mechanisms: the subvolume‑level visibility flag, client‑side enforcement, and the NFS share‑level toggle.

Subvolume‑level visibility 
Each CephFS subvolume maintains a visibility attribute.
 
```
ceph.subvolume.snaps.visible = {0|1}
```

- 1 (true) — the .snap directory is visible.
- 0 (false) — the .snap directory is hidden.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 When the flag is set to 0, clients that enforce visibility rules cannot view or access the .snap directory. These clients are also blocked from performing snapshot operations such as creation, deletion, cloning, or scheduling.

Client‑side visibility enforcement 
Clients enforce the subvolume visibility flag when the below configuration is enabled.
 
```
client_respect_subvolume_snapshot_visibility = true
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This setting must be applied to the specific CephX identity used by the CephFS or NFS client.

Share‑level snapshot visibility (NFS) 
For NFS clients, Ceph offers an additional share‑level toggle that controls .snap directory visibility on a per‑share basis.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Administrators can configure this toggle using:
 
- Ceph Dashboard (UI)
- Ceph NFS API

This share‑level setting works in combination with:

- the subvolume visibility flag,
- the client‑side enforcement configuration.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 All three mechanisms must align for NFS clients to observe the intended snapshot visibility behavior.
section_path: Snapshot visibility for CephFS and NFS clients > How snapshot visibility works at subvolume, client, and share levels

title: Configure snapshot (.snap) visibility for CephFS NFS shares
content: Control whether the CephFS .snap directory is visible and accessible for NFS clients on a per-share basis. This setting works with subvolume-level visibility flags and client-side configuration.
section_path: Configure snapshot (.snap) visibility for CephFS NFS shares

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Ensure a CephFS cluster with snapshots enabled.
- Configure an NFS cluster through the Ceph MGR NFS module or Ceph Dashboard.
- Have Ceph CLI access and valid CephX credentials for NFS clients.
section_path: Configure snapshot (.snap) visibility for CephFS NFS shares > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
The .snap directory is visible by default. You can control visibility based on the following:

- Subvolume-level flag: Indicates whether snapshots are visible for a specific subvolume.
- client-level flag: Determines whether the client enforces the subvolume and share snapshot visibility settings when accessing the .snap directory.
- Share-level toggle: Determines whether NFS shares expose the .snap directory.
- Whether the NFS client respects visibility settings.

The setting takes effect only when clients respect the subvolume visibility flag by enabling client_respect_subvolume_snapshot_visibility.
section_path: Configure snapshot (.snap) visibility for CephFS NFS shares > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Enable at subvolume-level
1. Set snapshot visibility for a subvolume.

```bash
ceph fs subvolume snap snapshot visibility set <fs_name> <subvolume_name> <subvolume_group> <true|false>
```

For example,
 
```
ceph fs subvolume snap snapshot visibility set cephfs sv1 appgrp false
```
2. (Optional) run the below command to set the extended attribute manually.

```bash
setfattr -n ceph.subvolume.snaps.visible -v 0 /cephfs/path/to/subvolume
```
Enable at client-level
1. Retrieve CephX identity.

```bash
ceph nfs export info <nfs-cluster-name> <export-pseudo-path>
```
2. Configure client-side respect for visibility flags.

```bash
ceph config set client.<cephx_entity> client_respect_subvolume_snapshot_visibility true
```

For example,
 
```
ceph config set client.nfs-cephx-user client_respect_subvolume_snapshot_visibility true
```
3. Verify if the flag visibility is configured.

```bash
ceph config get client.<cephx_entity> client_respect_subvolume_snapshot_visibility
```
Configure the share-level toggle. 
1. In the Ceph Dashboard, click **NFS** > **Exports**, then click **Create** or **Edit**. Toggle Snapshot (.snap) visibility, and click Save.
API example,
 
```
{
 "exportId": "exp-56789",
 "path": "/cephfs/subvolumes/teamB",
 "access": false
}
```
2. Verify on the NFS client.

```bash
mount -t nfs <nfs_server>:/exports/sv1 /mnt/sv1
ls -la /mnt/sv1
# access=true → .snap is visible
# access=false → .snap is hidden
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Attempting access if disabled returns EPERM.
section_path: Configure snapshot (.snap) visibility for CephFS NFS shares > Procedure

title: Results
content: Visibility of the .snap directory matches your configuration across subvolume, client, and share settings. Snapshot operations are blocked if visibility is disabled and clients enforce the visibility flag.
section_path: Configure snapshot (.snap) visibility for CephFS NFS shares > Results

title: Troubleshooting SMB in a Ceph environment
content:
Learn how to troubleshoot common SMB issues in a Ceph environment.

This section provides essential troubleshooting guidance for diagnosing and resolving issues that are related to SMB (Server Message Block) services in a Ceph environment. The troubleshooting focuses on three key areas: testing, measuring, and validating.

Testing client connectivity
Learn how to verify connectivity between the Windows client and Ceph SMB services by using basic network and share access checks. For more information, seeTesting connectivity of Ceph SMB services from the client side (Windows).
Measuring SMB throughput
Understand how to measure data transfer performance between the SMB share and the Windows client to identify any bottlenecks or inconsistencies. For more information, see Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy.
Validating VIPs and failover
Test the functions of Virtual IPs (VIPs) and ensure proper failover behavior if there is node or service disruptions to maintain high availability. For more information, see Testing Virtual IP and failovers.

These troubleshooting steps can help isolate issues, validate configurations, and ensure that the SMB integration in your Ceph cluster operates reliably and efficiently.
section_path: Troubleshooting SMB in a Ceph environment

title: Testing connectivity of Ceph SMB services from the client side (Windows)
content:
Learn about the SMB file system share access right and control management.

Clients can connect to the servers after a cluster and its component containers are deployed and the shares are configured. Microsoft Windows systems have SMB support that is built in and using Windows Explorer a share can be specified as: \\<hostname>\<sharename>. For example, \\ceph0.mycluster.sink.test\Staff Pics.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 IP addresses must be added in the DNS to use the hostnames.

 The Windows node automatically attempts to log in to the share. If the cluster and Windows client are configured for the same AD Domain, a password-less single sign-on login is automatically performed. A username and password prompt appears if the cluster is configured for user authentication. Enter one username and password combination that was specified in the cluster or the `ceph.smb.usersgroups` resource.

MacOS X systems and many Linux based systems also support connecting to SMB shares.
section_path: Testing connectivity of Ceph SMB services from the client side (Windows)

title: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy
content: Learn to measure SMB throughput between the SMB share and the Windows client by using the in-built robocopy utility in Windows.
section_path: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy

title: About this task
content: To assess the data transfer performance between the SMB share and the Windows client, use the built-in robocopy utility. This helps identify potential performance bottlenecks or latency issues in the SMB communication.
section_path: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. On the Windows client, open a command prompt with administrative privileges.
2. Run the following command to copy a large test file or directory from the local system to the mounted SMB share (or vice versa).

```bash
robocopy C:\path\to\source \\SMB_SERVER\sharename /E /Z /NP /R:0 /W:0 /LOG:robocopy_log.txt
```

Where,
 
C:\path\to\source
Is the path of the test data.
\\SMB_SERVER\sharename
Is the SMB share path.
/Z switch
The `/Z` switch enables restartable mode, `/NP` disables progress display for better performance, and `/LOG` logs the output.

The robocopy_log.txt is emitted to the path specified.
3. Check the log metrics.
After the robocopy log is emitted, check the file for the following metrics:
 
- Bytes transferred
- Transfer time
- Throughput (in MB/min)

These metrics can help determine whether throughput is within expected limits based on your network and storage setup. If performance is lesser than expected, investigate factors such as network latency, SMB version, or server-side resource constraints.
section_path: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy > Procedure

title: Troubleshooting TLS security in NFS
content:
Learn how to troubleshoot common TLS-related issues in NFS environments.

This section provides essential troubleshooting guidance for diagnosing and resolving issues that affect Transport Layer Security (TLS) when it is used to secure NFS communication. TLS protects NFS traffic by encrypting data in transit and validating identities during the TLS handshake. When TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS) is misconfigured, NFS clients may fail to mount shares or fall back to unencrypted communication.

Troubleshooting focuses on three key areas: validating, checking, and confirming the TLS configuration.

Validating TLS handshake and certificates 
Learn how to identify issues in the TLS handshake, such as invalid or expired certificates, missing CA trust, or incorrect identity fields that prevent secure channel establishment between the NFS client and server.
Checking authentication mode (TLS vs mTLS)
Understand how to verify whether the environment is configured for one-way TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS), and confirm that both the client and server provide certificates as expected during connection setup.
Confirming TLS configuration and transport settings
Review share security (XprtSec) settings, server policies, and client configuration, including Stunnel setups when applicable, to help ensure that TLS is correctly enforced and that NFS traffic is encrypted as intended.

These troubleshooting steps help isolate TLS negotiation issues, validate certificate and authentication settings, and ensure secure, encrypted NFS communication in your Ceph environment.
section_path: Troubleshooting TLS security in NFS

title: Setting up TLS in NFS clients using tlshd (ktls-utils)
content: Learn how to use tlshd (ktls-utils) to enable TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS) for NFS clients with native TLS capability.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS clients using tlshd (ktls-utils)

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Install TLS backend libraries (OpenSSL) based on your build configuration.
- Enable Kernel TLS (KTLS) if you are using OpenSSL and ktls.
- Generate and make accessible the TLS certificates and keys.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You must have access to the following TLS certificates:
 
- CA certificate (`ca.crt`)
- Server certificate (`ganesha.crt`)
- Private key (`ganesha.key`)
- Set correct file permissions for the certificate and key files so that NFS can access them.
- Ensure client-side support for TLS or mTLS (NFS client tools that support `xprtsec=tls` or `xprtsec=mtls`).
 
For more information on configuring the NFS client with TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS) support How to > Enhancing security > Data encryption in transit > Establishing encryption in transit for regional file share. > Establishing encryption in transit for regional file share in Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) documentation in IBM Cloud Docs.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS clients using tlshd (ktls-utils) > Before you begin

title: About this task
content: Enable TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS) for NFS clients using tlshd (ktls‑utils). Use this procedure when your environment supports native NFS TLS and you want to secure traffic without relying on external tunneling tools.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS clients using tlshd (ktls-utils) > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Install ktls-utils.
2. Configure `/etc/tlshd.conf` with TLS settings.
3. Start the tlshd service and mount the file share.

```bash
mount -vv -t nfs -o vers=4 -o xprtsec=mtls -o rw <server_ip>:/exportfs0 /mnt
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For native mount options, update the OS to the latest version because recent RHEL/CentOS kernels include TLS-related fixes.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS clients using tlshd (ktls-utils) > Procedure

title: Results
content:
When TLS or mTLS is enabled, NFS mounts use encrypted communication between the client and server, ensuring data confidentiality and integrity. TLS secures traffic and validates the server certificate. mTLS adds stronger authentication by validating both client and server certificates.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Incorrect settings, such as missing certificates or mismatched `xprtsec` options, cause mount failures with `EACCES` errors.
section_path: Setting up TLS in NFS clients using tlshd (ktls-utils) > Results

title: Manually configuring TLS settings for NFS
content: Diagnose and resolve issues that occur when enabling or using TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS) for NFS.
section_path: Manually configuring TLS settings for NFS

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- The NFS configuration file (`ganesha.conf`) is accessible for editing.
- You have administrative privileges to restart NFS services.
section_path: Manually configuring TLS settings for NFS > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
TLS settings in NFS define how encrypted communication is established between clients and the server. These parameters allow administrators to enable TLS, specify certificates, choose cipher suites, and configure advanced options such as Kernel TLS (KTLS) and debugging. This topic explains each configuration option and provides examples for OpenSSL backends.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The certificates required by the nfs service should be created by the user.

TLS configuration parameters and their default values are listed in Table 1.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
| --------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Enable_TLS | false | Enable or disable TLS support. |
| TLS_CA_File | "" | Path to CA certificate file. |
| TLS_Cert_File | "" | Path to server certificate file. |
| TLS_Key_File | "" | Path to private key file. |
| TLS_Ciphers | NULL | Specify cipher suites for TLS. |
| TLS_Min_Version | TLSv1.3 | Minimum TLS protocol version. |
| Enable_KTLS | false | Enable Kernel TLS (OpenSSL only). |
| Enable_debug | false | Enable detailed TLS debugging logs. |
section_path: Manually configuring TLS settings for NFS > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Enable TLS support in the `TLS_CONFIG{}` block.

```bash
Enable_TLS = true
```
2. Specify certificate file paths.

```bash
TLS_CA_File = "/etc/ganesha/tls/ca.crt"
TLS_Cert_File = "/etc/ganesha/tls/ganesha.crt"
TLS_Key_File = "/etc/ganesha/tls/ganesha.key"
```
3. Configure the cipher suites, for OpenSSL.

```bash
TLS_Ciphers = "TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384"
```
4. Set the minimum TLS version.

```
TLS_Min_Version = "TLSv1.3"
```
5. Enable Kernel TLS (KTLS) for OpenSSL.

```bash
Enable_KTLS = true
```
6. Enable debugging for detailed TLS logs.

```bash
Enable_debug = true
```
section_path: Manually configuring TLS settings for NFS > Procedure

title: Manually specify share security options for NFS
content: Configure NFS share security settings directly in the Ceph NFS service configuration files when you need fine‑grained control over encryption requirements. This method is useful when managing complex deployments, custom TLS setups, or when avoiding command‑line defaults.
section_path: Manually specify share security options for NFS

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Administrative privileges to modify share configurations.
- The TLS backend can be OpenSSL. This is a compile-time option.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 To enable TLS support in NFS, you must select `USE_OPENSSL` for OpenSSL backend during compile time.
section_path: Manually specify share security options for NFS > Before you begin

title: About this task
content: NFS share security settings directly in the NFS share files. It provides guidance on selecting TLS or mutual TLS (mTLS) requirements, defining TLS parameters such as certificates and cipher policies, and preparing the environment for secure NFS access.
section_path: Manually specify share security options for NFS > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Specify the share security option in the `EXPORT{}` or `EXPORT_DEFAULTS{}` block.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You can specify only one share security option, XprtSec = tls or mtls.

For example,
 
```
XprtSec = tls
```
2. Specify the TLS configuration parameters in the `TLS_CONFIG{}` block.

```bash
Enable_TLS = true
TLS_CA_File = "/etc/ganesha/tls/ca.crt"
TLS_Cert_File = "/etc/ganesha/tls/ganesha.crt"
TLS_Key_File = "/etc/ganesha/tls/ganesha.key"
TLS_Ciphers = "TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384"
TLS_Min_Version = "TLSv1.3"
Enable_KTLS = true
Enable_debug = false
```
section_path: Manually specify share security options for NFS > Procedure

title: Results
content:
After setting the TLS configuration, the Ceph command changes.

```
ceph nfs export create cephfs mynfs /export3 myfs --xprtsec tls
```
section_path: Manually specify share security options for NFS > Results
